name: Veredas Bible Dictionary
credit: Veredas Bible Dictionary. Short introductory entries, neutral among the Christian traditions. Translated from the Portuguese original.
entries: Brother of Moses, his spokesman before Pharaoh and the first high priest of Israel. The priestly line descends from him.
Aramaic word meaning "father," of filial intimacy. Jesus used it when praying in Gethsemane, and Paul says that the Spirit makes us cry "Abba, Father."
Second son of Adam and Eve, a shepherd. His offering was accepted by God, and he was killed by Cain. Hebrews cites him as an example of faith.
Priest, sole survivor of Saul's slaughter of the priests of Nob, who joined David. He supported Adonijah against Solomon and was deposed.
Wife of Nabal and then of David, who prevented a massacre by bringing provisions to the future king.
King of Judah, son of Rehoboam, who reigned three years. Before a battle against Jeroboam, he gave a speech recalling that Judah had remained faithful to the Lord and to the temple.

Name of more than one figure. The oldest is the Philistine king of Gerar, who took Sarah thinking she was Abraham's sister and later made a covenant with Abraham and with Isaac. Another Abimelech was a son of Gideon, who made himself king of Shechem after killing his brothers.
Nephew of David, son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab, a valiant chief of his warriors. He wanted to kill Saul and later Shimei, but David stopped him.
Commander of Saul's army and his cousin, who supported Ish-bosheth and later went over to David's side. He was killed by Joab in Hebron.

Patriarch of Israel and "father of many nations". Called by God in Ur of the Chaldeans, he set out for Canaan with the promise of a land, of descendants, and of blessing for all the families of the earth. He is remembered as a model of faith, and his original name, Abram, was changed by God.
Son of David who conspired against his father and proclaimed himself king. He was killed by Joab after being caught by his hair in an oak tree.
Desert tree with hard and durable wood. It was used to make the ark of the covenant, the table and the altar of the tabernacle.
Roman province of southern Greece, including Athens and Corinth.
Israelite who, at Jericho, took spoils consecrated to God and hid them. The sin caused the defeat at Ai, and Achan was stoned in the valley of Achor.
Philistine king of Gath, with whom David took refuge when fleeing from Saul.
Second volume of Luke's work. It tells of the ascension of Jesus, Pentecost, the expansion of the church from Jerusalem to Rome and the work of Peter and Paul.

First man according to Genesis, formed from the dust of the ground and placed by God in the garden of Eden. His name comes from the Hebrew word for "humanity" and "ground". The New Testament presents him as the head of humanity, in contrast with Christ.
Hebrew word that means "my Lord". It is the term read in place of the divine name YHWH, and is usually translated "Lord".
King of Jerusalem, leader of the coalition of five Amorite kings against Gibeon, defeated by Joshua on the day the sun stood still.
Son of David who tried to take the throne while his father was old, but Solomon was anointed king. He was later executed by Solomon.
Act by which someone becomes a child of a family. In the New Testament, it describes how Christians are welcomed as children of God through Christ, and may call him "Abba, Father".
City of Judah with a cave where David took refuge when fleeing from Saul and where many malcontents gathered.

Sexual relation of a married person with someone who is not the spouse, forbidden by the seventh commandment. Jesus says that adultery also begins in the heart, but he forgave the woman caught in adultery.
Someone who speaks on behalf of another. John calls Jesus an "advocate with the Father" and calls the Holy Spirit the "Paraclete", a word also translated Comforter, Helper or Counselor.
King of the Amalekites, spared by Saul against God's command. Samuel executed him, and Saul was rejected as king.
Greek word for "love," above all God's love and selfless love. In Jude and in Corinthians, it also appears for the fraternal meal of Christians, the "love feast."
King of Israel, married to Jezebel. He promoted the worship of Baal and was rebuked by Elijah, above all over the matter of Naboth's vineyard.
King of Persia, husband of Esther, whom historical tradition identifies with Xerxes I. His kingdom ran "from India to Ethiopia", in one hundred twenty-seven provinces.
King of Judah, son of Jotham, an idolater, who refused to ask for a sign and sought help from Assyria. It was to him that Isaiah announced the sign of Immanuel.
Name of two kings: Ahaziah of Israel, son of Ahab, who died after a fall, and Ahaziah of Judah, grandson of Ahab, killed by Jehu.
Prophet of Shiloh who tore his cloak into twelve pieces and gave ten to Jeroboam, announcing the division of the kingdom. Later he announced judgment on Jeroboam's house.
Counselor of David, famous for his wisdom, who went over to Absalom's side in the revolt. When his counsel was rejected, he hanged himself.
City of Canaan, near Bethel, defeated by Joshua after the sin of Achan was dealt with.
Great city of Egypt, a center of culture, with a large Jewish community. The Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, was made there. Apollos was from this city.
Aromatic substance used in perfumes and in burial. Nicodemus brought myrrh and aloes to embalm the body of Jesus.
First and last letters of the Greek alphabet. In Revelation, it is a title of God and of Christ, meaning "the beginning and the end, the first and the last".
Structure of stone, earth or bronze on which sacrifices were offered. The patriarchs raised altars where God appeared to them. The tabernacle had the altar of burnt offering and that of incense.

Small altar of acacia wood overlaid with gold, in the holy place, before the veil, where incense was burned morning and evening. Luke tells that Zechariah was offering incense when the angel appeared to him.
Nomadic people of the Negev desert, who attacked Israel after the exodus. Saul was rejected for not carrying out God's command against them.
King of Judah and father of Uzziah. He defeated Edom, but brought home the gods of the conquered and was defeated by Joash of Israel.
Hebrew word meaning "so be it" or "firm, true", used to confirm a prayer or declaration. Jesus used it at the beginning of solemn statements, translated "truly".
People east of the Jordan, descended from Lot, often in conflict with Israel.
Firstborn of David, who violated his half-sister Tamar and was killed by Absalom's order.

People of Canaan and of Transjordan, linked to several city-states. The Amorite kings Sihon and Og were defeated by Israel east of the Jordan. In Genesis, the iniquity of the Amorites "is not yet full".
Shepherd and tender of sycamore figs from Tekoa, called as a prophet to denounce social injustice in the northern kingdom.
People of great stature who lived in Hebron and in southern Canaan. The spies sent by Moses felt like grasshoppers before them. Joshua and Caleb drove them out.
Name of several people in the New Testament: the husband who, with his wife, lied to the church, the disciple in Damascus who welcomed Saul, and a high priest who put him on trial.
Couple of Jerusalem who sold a piece of land, kept back part of the price and lied to Peter, saying they had given everything. Both died, and great fear came upon the church.
Fisherman, brother of Simon Peter and disciple of John the Baptist before following Jesus. He brought to the Lord the boy with the five loaves and some Greeks.
Relatives and fellow prisoners of Paul, whom Romans calls "notable among the apostles" and who were in Christ before him.
Word meaning "messenger". Spiritual beings in the service of God, who carry messages, protect and praise. They appear from Genesis to Revelation.
Elderly widow who served in the temple and spoke of the child Jesus to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
Former high priest, father-in-law of Caiaphas, with great influence in the temple. Jesus was taken to him first after his arrest.
Visit of the angel Gabriel to Mary, in Nazareth, announcing that she would conceive and give birth to Jesus, the Son of the Most High, by the power of the Holy Spirit.
Pouring oil on someone to consecrate them to a role, such as king, priest or prophet, or to heal. The Messiah is the "Anointed One".
Act of pouring oil on someone to consecrate him, as priest, king or prophet. "Messiah" and "Christ" mean "anointed". The New Testament also speaks of anointing by the Spirit.

Term used in John's letters for whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ and for the spirit of opposition to him. John says that "many antichrists" had already appeared. Christian tradition also associates the term with a final figure of deception.
City in Syria, where the disciples were first called "Christians". It was the base of Paul's missionary journeys.
City of Galatia where Paul preached in the synagogue and, rejected, turned to the Gentiles. It is distinct from Antioch of Syria.
Greek word meaning "revelation". It gives its name to the last book of the Bible and to a symbolic literary genre, also present in Daniel and Ezekiel.
Ancient Jewish books, written largely between the Old and New Testaments, such as Tobit, Judith and Maccabees. Christian traditions differ as to their acceptance in the canon.
Jew of Alexandria, eloquent and well versed in the Scriptures, who taught in Ephesus and Corinth after being instructed by Priscilla and Aquila.
Abandonment of the faith one professed. Paul speaks of a falling away that comes before the day of the Lord, and Hebrews warns against turning away from the living God.
Greek word meaning "sent one". It designates the twelve chosen by Jesus and, in a broader sense, other missionaries such as Paul and Barnabas.
Jew born in Pontus, a tentmaker like Paul and husband of Priscilla. Expelled from Rome, they welcomed Paul in Corinth and instructed Apollos in Ephesus.
Deep valley that runs from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea and beyond. The Dead Sea is called the "sea of the Arabah."
Peninsula south and east of Canaan. Paul spent some time in Arabia after his conversion.
Mountain range where, according to Genesis, Noah's ark came to rest after the flood.
"Chief angel." The Bible uses the word twice: Paul says that the Lord will descend "with the voice of an archangel," and Jude calls Michael an archangel.
Hill of Athens, and also the council that met there. Paul spoke there about the "unknown God".

Box of acacia wood overlaid with gold, which held the tablets of the Law. It stood in the most holy place of the tabernacle, with the lid called the mercy seat, a symbol of God's presence among the people.
Paul's image for the believer's spiritual resources: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God.
River and valley that separated Moab from the Amorites, the northern border of Moab.
Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane, at night, after Judas's betrayal, by soldiers and temple guards. The disciples fled, and Peter denied him three times.
King of Persia who, in his seventh year, authorized Ezra to return to Jerusalem and, in his twentieth, sent Nehemiah to rebuild the walls.
Greek goddess of hunting and fertility, whose great temple was at Ephesus. The silversmith Demetrius stirred up the riot against Paul, fearing to lose the business of the shrines.
King of Judah who removed the idols and restored worship, but at the end of his life trusted in the king of Syria and not in the Lord.
Levite, musician and singer from the time of David, tied to worship. Twelve psalms are attributed to him (50 and 73-83), and his descendants formed a guild of singers.
Ascent of Jesus into heaven, forty days after the resurrection, before his disciples.
Egyptian wife of Joseph, daughter of the priest Potiphera of On, whom Pharaoh gave him. She was the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim.
Philistine city where the ark was placed in the temple of Dagon, whose statue fell before it. Nehemiah mentions it for the language of its inhabitants.
Eighth son of Jacob, second of Zilpah. The name recalls "happy". The tribe occupied the northern coast, near Tyre and Sidon.
Philistine coastal city, mentioned by David in the lament for Saul and Jonathan and by the prophets.

Canaanite goddess of love and fertility, venerated with Baal. Asherah was the name of a goddess and of the sacred poles dedicated to her, which the prophets and reforming kings ordered to be torn down.
Roman province in the west of present-day Turkey, with Ephesus as capital. In it stood the seven churches of Revelation.
Small Roman copper coin, a sixteenth of a denarius. Jesus says that two sparrows are sold for an assarion.
Empire of northern Mesopotamia that destroyed the kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and threatened Judah.
Queen of Judah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, who seized the throne and had the royal family put to death.
Greek city of great philosophical tradition, where Paul spoke at the Areopagus about the "unknown God".

Act that removes guilt and restores the relationship with God. In the Old Testament it was tied to the sacrifices and to the Day of Atonement. The New Testament applies the idea to the death of Christ.

Close relative who, according to the law, had to avenge the death of a family member. The cities of refuge protected those who had killed by accident. The same Hebrew term, go'el, means "redeemer", as Boaz was for Ruth.
Canaanite god of rain and fertility, whose name means "lord." The Israelites often turned aside to worship him. Elijah's confrontation on Mount Carmel showed that only the LORD is God.

City in Shinar where, according to Genesis, people tried to build a tower up to heaven. God confused their languages and scattered the people. The name is tied to the Hebrew word for "confusion". It is the same root as Babylon.
Capital of the Babylonian empire, which destroyed Jerusalem and took the Jews into exile. In the New Testament the name appears with a symbolic sense for an oppressive and sinful power.
Diviner summoned by the king of Moab to curse Israel, but who ended up blessing the people. His donkey spoke when it saw him.
King of Moab who hired Balaam to curse Israel, but who heard only blessings.
Medicinal resin produced in Gilead, used to treat wounds. Jeremiah asks: "Is there no balm in Gilead?", as an image of the healing of a wounded people.

Rite of immersion or washing with water. John the Baptist baptized for repentance; Jesus was baptized by him. The early church baptized those who believed. The different Christian traditions differ on the mode and the timing.
Notorious prisoner whom the crowd asked to be released in place of Jesus.
Israelite general who, at Deborah's request, gathered ten thousand men and defeated Sisera's army. Hebrews cites him among those who acted by faith.
Cereal that ripens earlier than wheat, the basis of the bread of the poor. The boy who gave five barley loaves to Jesus appears in the account of the multiplication.
Jew from Cyprus called "son of encouragement", who introduced Paul to the church in Jerusalem and was his first companion in mission, before they parted over John Mark.
Parable of the owner who wants to cut down the fig tree that bears no fruit, and of the vinedresser who asks for one more year. It speaks of God's patience and of the need for fruits of repentance.
Surname of two men of the early church: Joseph Barsabbas, called Justus, candidate to replace Judas, and Judas Barsabbas, a prophet sent from Jerusalem to Antioch with Silas.
Apostle, usually identified with Nathanael of Cana, whom Jesus called "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit".
Blind beggar of Jericho, son of Timaeus, who cried out to Jesus and received his sight.
Scribe and secretary of Jeremiah, who wrote down the prophet's words and read them in the temple. He accompanied him in hard times.
Elderly and wealthy Gileadite who supported David and his men at Mahanaim during Absalom's revolt. David wanted to reward him, but he preferred to stay at home.
Fertile region east of the Jordan and north of Gilead, known for its oaks and sturdy cattle. It was the kingdom of Og, defeated by Moses.
Liquid measure equal to the ephah, about twenty-two liters. In Solomon's temple, the "molten sea" held about two thousand baths.
Wife of Uriah whom David took and whose husband he had killed. After the king's repentance she became the mother of Solomon.
Wild animal that David faced while guarding sheep. It appears in visions of Daniel as an image of a kingdom.

In Revelation, the beast is a power that opposes God and demands worship, with a number, 666. Ancient and modern Christians associate it with Rome, with oppressive powers or with a future figure. Interpreters differ.
Declaration of happiness or blessing upon someone. The beatitudes of Jesus open the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew) and the Sermon on the Plain (Luke). They also appear in the Psalms.
Name given to the chief of the demons. The adversaries of Jesus accused him of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul. The name comes from Baal-zebub, god of Ekron.
City at the far south of Canaan, tied to Abraham and Isaac, who dug wells there and made a covenant. The expression "from Dan to Beersheba" designates the whole territory of Israel.
Small weights of the shekel: the beka is half a shekel, and the gerah is a twentieth. Used in the tabernacle for the ransom tax.
Chief gods of Babylon, whom the prophets describe as humiliated, carried on carts and defeated, since they cannot save.
Hebrew word for "worthlessness" or "wickedness." "Sons of Belial" are perverse people. Paul uses "Beliar" as the name of the power of evil in opposition to Christ.
King of Babylon at whose banquet the mysterious writing appeared on the wall. Daniel interpreted it, and that very night the kingdom was taken.
Name of kings of Damascus (Syria), at war with Israel since the days of Ahab.
Chief of David's personal guard and valiant warrior. In Solomon's reign he became commander of the army.
Song of Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, after the birth of his son. It praises God for salvation and announces John's mission as forerunner.
Youngest son of Jacob and Rachel, whom his mother named Ben-oni as she was dying. The tribe of Benjamin was that of Saul, the first king of Israel, and of the apostle Paul.
City of Macedonia where the Jews received Paul's word with great interest and examined the Scriptures daily.
Sister of Herod Agrippa II, who accompanied him at the hearing in which Paul defended himself in Caesarea.
City of Judah to which the ark returned from the Philistines; its inhabitants were punished for looking at it irreverently.
Village near Jerusalem, where Martha, Mary and Lazarus lived. There is another Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John baptized.
Place where Jacob dreamed of the ladder and called the place "house of God". Later it became a sanctuary of the northern kingdom.
Pool in Jerusalem, with five porches, where many sick people waited. Jesus healed there a man who had been paralyzed for thirty-eight years.
City a few miles from Jerusalem, where David was born and where, according to Matthew and Luke, Jesus was born. Its name means "house of bread".
Village on the Mount of Olives, from where Jesus sent for the colt to enter Jerusalem.
City of Galilee by the sea, home of Peter, Andrew and Philip. Jesus healed a blind man there, and nearby he multiplied the loaves.
Craftsman of the tribe of Judah, filled with the Spirit of God with wisdom and skill to make the tabernacle and its utensils, assisted by Oholiab.

Collection of sacred books of Judaism (Old Testament) and of Christianity (Old and New Testaments). The name comes from the Greek "biblia", "books". The Protestant canon has 66 books; Catholics and Orthodox include other books, called deuterocanonical.
Maidservants given to Jacob as secondary wives, Bilhah by Rachel and Zilpah by Leah. From Bilhah were born Dan and Naphtali; from Zilpah, Gad and Asher.

Account by Matthew and Luke of the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, in the time of the census of Augustus: the manger, the angels and the shepherds, then the magi. The date of December 25 comes from later tradition; the Bible does not record it.
Dark and sticky substance, used for waterproofing. Noah used it in the ark and the basket of Moses was sealed with pitch. At Babel, it was used as mortar.
Disrespect toward God or sacred things, in word or action. Jesus was accused of blasphemy by the leaders. He also spoke of "blasphemy against the Spirit", which would not be forgiven.

Word of good that invokes or declares God's favor on someone. God blesses Abraham so that he may be a blessing to all peoples, and Jesus blesses the children. The Bible also speaks of blessing God, in praise.

In the Bible, a symbol of life, which belongs to God. In the sacrifices, the blood made atonement. In the New Testament, the blood of Christ is the basis of forgiveness, of the new covenant and of redemption.
Close relative of Naomi who, as a kinsman-redeemer, married Ruth. He was the great-grandfather of David and is remembered in the genealogy of Jesus.
Image used by Paul for the church, in which each member has a distinct function and all form one body.
Book in which are written the names of those who belong to God. It appears in the Old Testament, in the letters of Paul and in Revelation.
Two books that retell the history of Israel starting from Adam, with emphasis on David, the temple and worship, written after the exile to encourage the restored community.
Two books that tell the history of the kings of Israel and of Judah, from Solomon and the building of the temple to the exile, with the prophets Elijah and Elisha.
Two books that tell of the end of the period of the judges and the rise of the monarchy: Samuel, Saul and David.
Basic food, made of wheat or barley. In the Bible, "bread" can mean food in general. Jesus said: "Man shall not live by bread alone" and "I am the bread of life".
Twelve loaves placed every week on a gold table in the holy place, before God. Only the priests could eat them. Jesus recalled the case in which David ate them.
Piece of the high priest's dress, with twelve precious stones that represented the twelve tribes of Israel.
Metal used in the tabernacle, in weapons and in utensils, such as the bronze altar and the bronze serpent.
Large bronze vessel, in the court of the tabernacle, where the priests washed before serving. In Solomon's temple, there was the "sea of cast metal".
Serpent that Moses made in the wilderness, by God's order, so that those bitten by venomous snakes could look at it and live. Jesus compares it to himself, "lifted up" on the cross.
Shrub that burned without being consumed, where God appeared to Moses at Horeb and revealed his name.
Sacrifice in which the animal was completely burned on the altar, as an offering of total dedication to God.

Title of the Roman emperors. Augustus decreed the census of Luke 2; Tiberius reigned during Jesus' ministry ("Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's"); Claudius expelled Jews from Rome; Nero is the emperor to whom Paul appealed.
Roman port on the coast of Israel, seat of the Roman government. Cornelius lived there and Paul was held prisoner there.
Port city built by Herod the Great in honor of Caesar, residence of the Roman governor. Philip and Cornelius lived there, and Paul was held prisoner there for two years.
City at the foot of Mount Hermon, where Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ.
High priest in the time of Jesus, son-in-law of Annas, who presided over the trial before the Sanhedrin and argued that it was better for one man to die for the people.

First son of Adam and Eve, a farmer. Out of jealousy he killed his brother Abel, and God marked him so that he would not be killed in revenge. The New Testament remembers him as an example of envy and violence.
Spy from the tribe of Judah who, with Joshua, trusted that Israel would conquer Canaan. For his faithfulness he received Hebron as an inheritance.
God's invitation to someone to a mission or relationship. It appears in the calling of Abraham, Moses, the prophets and the disciples. In the New Testament, all Christians are "called" to holiness.
Pack animal of the desert. Jesus says that it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom, and John the Baptist wore clothing of camel's hair.
Village of Galilee, where Jesus turned water into wine, in his first sign.
Land promised to Abraham and his descendants, between the Jordan and the Mediterranean. Also the name of a son of Ham, ancestor of the Canaanites.
Foreign woman from the region of Tyre and Sidon, whose daughter Jesus healed after admiring her persistent faith.

Peoples who lived in the land of Canaan before Israel, with a religion tied to Baal and Asherah. In the New Testament, the woman who asked for her daughter's healing is called Canaanite or Syrophoenician.
List of books recognized as Scripture. The Greek word means "rule". Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants differ over the books of the Old Testament.
City on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, base of Jesus' ministry, where Peter and other disciples lived.
Regions of Asia Minor. Peter writes to the "pilgrims scattered" in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia. There were people from there in Jerusalem at Pentecost.
Mountain range by the Mediterranean, where Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal.
Tall tree with fragrant and durable wood, a symbol of majesty and firmness. Solomon used cedars of Lebanon to build the temple and the palace.
Counting of the population. David took a census that displeased God. Luke links the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem to a census ordered by Augustus.

Roman officer who commanded a hundred soldiers. The centurion of Capernaum trusted that Jesus could heal his servant from a distance; another, at the foot of the cross, recognized: "Truly this was the Son of God". Cornelius, in Acts, is another centurion.
People of southern Mesopotamia, with Babylon as capital. Abraham came from "Ur of the Chaldeans".
God of the Moabites. Solomon built a shrine for him in Jerusalem, and Josiah destroyed it.
Beings of the heavenly world associated with the presence of God. They guarded Eden, were carved on the ark and appear in the visions of Ezekiel.
City of Galilee, near Capernaum, which Jesus rebuked for not repenting in the face of his miracles.
Title of Jesus, from the Greek Christos, "anointed", equivalent to the Hebrew "Messiah". It came to be used almost as a name: Jesus Christ.
Follower of Christ. According to Acts, the name arose in Antioch, used from the outside, and was later adopted by the disciples themselves.

Word that comes from the Greek "ekklesia", "called-out assembly". In the New Testament it designates the community of the followers of Christ, both the local congregations and the whole body of believers.
Province in southeastern Asia Minor, of which Tarsus was the principal city.

Cutting of the foreskin, sign of God's covenant with Abraham and practice of all the boys of Israel. In the New Testament, the question of requiring it of the Gentiles was settled at the council of Jerusalem.

Reservoir dug to store water, essential in a land of little rain. Wells were valuable, and the dispute over them appears in the stories of Abraham and Isaac. Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman by Jacob's well.

Six cities designated in the law, where someone who killed another by accident could take shelter until judged, protected from the avenger of blood. They were Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth and Golan.
Jebusite fortress of Zion that David took and made his capital, the oldest part of Jerusalem. In Luke, the name is also applied to Bethlehem.

Israel's law distinguished what was "clean" and "unclean" in foods, diseases, contacts and childbirth. These rules taught holiness, and ritual purity was restored through rites. Jesus insisted that what defiles comes from the heart.

Episode in which Jesus drove out of the temple those who sold animals and changed money, saying that the house of his Father was a house of prayer. John places it at the beginning of the ministry; the other Gospels, near the end.

Co-worker of Paul at Philippi, whose name is "in the book of life". A later tradition associates him with Clement of Rome, author of a letter to the Corinthians, though it cannot be affirmed that he is the same man.
Disciple who, with another, was walking to Emmaus when the risen Christ joined them.
Common garments of the time. The cloak was a piece worn for covering, which the creditor had to return at nightfall. The soldiers cast lots for the seamless tunic of Jesus.

Sign of God's presence: the pillar of cloud guided Israel in the wilderness and the cloud filled the tabernacle. Jesus ascended in a cloud, and at the transfiguration a cloud overshadowed the disciples.
Offering that Paul organized among the Gentile churches to help the poor Christians of Jerusalem, as a sign of fellowship between Jews and Gentiles.
City of Phrygia, to whose church Paul wrote a letter.
Comfort given in the midst of pain. The Bible presents God as the "Father of mercies and God of all comfort", who comforts so that believers can comfort others.

The ten commandments, engraved on stone tablets on Mount Sinai, sum up Israel's obligations toward God and neighbor. They are repeated in Deuteronomy, and Jesus summed them up in the double commandment of love.

Act of acknowledging sin before God, and sometimes before others, or of declaring one's faith. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins." It also means the profession of faith: "Jesus is Lord".
Inner capacity to discern right from wrong. Paul describes it as an inner witness that can be strong or weak, and speaks of keeping "a good conscience".
Change of direction, turning back to God. The New Testament links it to repentance and faith. Christians differ on how it occurs, but agree that it involves new life.

Encounter of Saul, persecutor of the church, with the risen Lord, in a bright light, on the way to Damascus. He was blind for three days, was baptized by Ananias and began to preach that Jesus is the Son of God.
Hebrew word for "offering dedicated to God." Jesus criticized those who used corban as a pretext for not helping their parents.
Port city of Greece, where Paul founded a church and to which he wrote two letters.
Roman centurion of Caesarea, a God-fearer, to whom Peter announced the gospel. His conversion marks the opening of the church to the Gentiles.
Main stone at the angle of a building, which supports the construction. Psalm 118 speaks of the stone that the builders rejected, and the New Testament applies it to Christ.

Meeting of the apostles and elders to decide whether converted Gentiles needed to be circumcised. They concluded that they did not, asking only that they abstain from certain practices tied to idolatry and immorality.
Open area around the tabernacle and the temple, where the altar of burnt offering and the bronze basin stood. In Herod's temple, there was also the court of the Gentiles.

Solemn commitment between God and his people, with promises and responsibilities. The Bible speaks of covenants with Noah, Abraham, Moses and David, and announces a "new covenant", which Christianity associates with Christ.

Disordered desire for what belongs to others or for material goods, forbidden by the tenth commandment. Paul says that covetousness is idolatry, and Jesus warns: "Beware, and keep yourselves from covetousness."
God's work in making the world and everything that exists. Genesis opens the Bible with creation, and many texts praise the Creator. Christians differ on how to interpret the details of the account.
Inhabitants of Crete. Paul quotes a Cretan poet who calls them liars, and writes to Titus about the churches of the island.
Island in the Mediterranean. Paul passed by there on the voyage to Rome, and left Titus to organize the churches of the island.
Ruler of the synagogue in Corinth who believed in the Lord with all his household and was baptized.
Roman instrument of execution, on which Jesus was put to death. For Christians it became a symbol of sacrifice and salvation.
Deliverance of Israel from Egypt, when the waters opened so that the people could pass on dry ground and closed over the army of Pharaoh. It is the great act of salvation remembered at Passover.
Sign of royalty, honor or victory. Paul speaks of the "crown of righteousness", and James and Revelation promise "the crown of life" to the faithful.
Crown of thorns placed on the head of Jesus by the Roman soldiers, in mockery of his kingship, before the crucifixion.

Form of Roman execution on the cross. Jesus was crucified at Golgotha, under Pontius Pilate, between two criminals, and died around the ninth hour. Christians see in it the sacrifice that atones for sin.

Ancient measure of length, equivalent to the forearm, from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger: about 45 centimeters (18 inches). It was used to measure Noah's ark, the tabernacle and the temple.
Word that declares or invokes evil on someone or something. In the law, the curse is the consequence of breaking the covenant. Paul says that Christ became a curse for us on the cross.
Region south of Egypt, on the upper Nile, called Cush in Hebrew and translated as Ethiopia. The eunuch baptized by Philip came from there.
Metal plates struck together, used in the worship of the temple. Paul says that without love he is like "a clanging cymbal".
Island in the Mediterranean, homeland of Barnabas, visited by Paul and Barnabas on the first journey.
City on the coast of Libya, from which Simon came, who carried Jesus' cross. There was a Jewish community there.
King of Persia who conquered Babylon and allowed the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. Isaiah calls him the Lord's anointed.
God of the Philistines. When the ark of the covenant was placed in his temple at Ashdod, the statue fell before it. At Gaza, Samson brought down the temple of Dagon.
Capital of Syria, on the road to which Saul met Jesus. There Paul was baptized and began to preach.

Fifth son of Jacob, first of Bilhah, and the tribe that descended from him. Part of the tribe settled in the far north, taking Laish, which came to be called Dan. The expression "from Dan to Beersheba" came to designate the whole territory of Israel.
Young Jew taken into exile in Babylon, who served in the court, interpreted dreams and remained faithful to God, even in the lions' den. His book contains visions of the end of time.
Persian gold coin, used in the time of the exile and the return. The heads of Israel contributed thousands of darics to the temple.

Name of kings. The "Mede" appears in Daniel as the king who succeeded Babylon and threw Daniel into the lions' den. The Darius of the time of Haggai and Zechariah is Darius I of Persia, who authorized the completion of the temple.

Image of the absence of light, used for evil, ignorance and judgment. In creation, God separates the light from the darkness. John says that the light shines in the darkness and the darkness has not overcome it.

Second king of Israel, a shepherd from Bethlehem, conqueror of Goliath, musician and poet, to whom many Psalms are attributed. He made Jerusalem the capital. God promised him an eternal house and throne, a promise the New Testament links to Jesus.

Most solemn day of the Jewish calendar, on which the high priest entered the most holy place and made atonement for the people, and a fast was observed. Hebrews compares this rite to the work of Christ.

Two different ideas. In the Old Testament, the "day of the LORD" is the day of God's intervention in judgment and deliverance. In the New, "Lord's day" is also applied to Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and "day of the Lord" appears as the coming of Christ.
From the Greek "servant". In Acts, the seven chosen to serve tables, and later a recognized ministry in the churches.
Sea of very salty water in the Jordan valley, also called the Salt Sea. It is the lowest point on earth. According to tradition, Sodom and Gomorrah were around it.
Prophetess and judge of Israel, who went with the general Barak to victory over Sisera's army. Her song is one of the oldest poetic texts in the Bible.
Region of ten cities of Greek culture, east of the Jordan, where Jesus healed the demon-possessed man of Gerasa.
Agile animal of the mountains and a symbol of longing and beauty. The psalmist compares his thirst for God to that of the deer that pants for streams of water.
Woman whom Samson loved, bribed by the Philistines to discover the secret of his strength and hand him over.
Co-worker of Paul, mentioned alongside Luke, who later deserted him "having loved this present world".
Name of two figures: a Christian praised in 3 John "by everyone and by the truth itself", and the silversmith of Ephesus who stirred up the riot against Paul because of the shrines of Artemis.
Evil spirits, which in the gospels afflict people and are cast out by Jesus and the disciples.
Roman silver coin, a day's wages. It appears in the parable of the workers in the vineyard and in the episode of the tax to Caesar.
City of Lycaonia, last stop of Paul's first missionary journey; home of Gaius.

Books of the Old Testament accepted as Scripture by Catholics and Orthodox, but not included in the Hebrew and Protestant canon: Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and parts of Esther and Daniel. Protestants call them apocrypha. See "Apocrypha".
Fifth book of the Bible, whose name means "second law". It gathers the farewell speeches of Moses, repeats the law, presents the Shema and prepares the people for life in the promised land.
Name of the spiritual being who opposes God and tempts human beings. The Greek word means "slanderer". He appears under names such as Satan, the Tempter, the Evil One and the ancient serpent.

Jews who lived outside the land of Israel, scattered among the nations since the exile. James and Peter write to Christians "of the Dispersion." In Jerusalem, at Pentecost, there were Jews from many places.
Daughter of Jacob and Leah. What happened to her in Shechem, where she was violated by the son of Hamor, led to the vengeance of her brothers Simeon and Levi.
Member of the Areopagus of Athens who believed after Paul's speech. He appears with a woman named Damaris.
Man who "loved to be first" in the church, refused the envoys of the apostle John and expelled those who received them.
Ability to distinguish right from wrong, true from false. The New Testament asks believers to "test the spirits" and to examine everything. In Hebrews, discernment develops with practice.
One who follows a teacher in order to learn from him. In the gospels it designates the followers of Jesus, who invited them to "make disciples of all nations".

Division of Solomon's kingdom after his death, around 930 BC. Ten tribes formed the kingdom of Israel, in the north, under Jeroboam; Judah and Benjamin formed the kingdom of Judah, in the south, with the dynasty of David. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC; the southern one, to Babylon in 586 BC.
Edomite, chief of Saul's herdsmen, who denounced the priest Ahimelech and killed eighty-five priests of Nob.
Animal considered unclean, often seen as contemptible. Jesus used the image in a conversation with the Canaanite woman. Paul and Revelation apply it to false teachers.
Pack animal, a symbol of humility. Jesus entered Jerusalem riding a colt. Balaam heard the donkey speak.
Place in northern Canaan where Joseph found his brothers and was sold to Ishmaelite merchants.

Bird, a symbol of peace, purity and simplicity. Noah's dove brought the olive branch, and the Spirit descended on Jesus "like a dove" at his baptism. Turtledoves and young pigeons were the offering of the poor.
Greek silver coin, of value close to the denarius. In Luke's parable, the woman searches for a lost drachma.
Parable in which a net cast into the sea gathers good and bad fish, and the bad are separated at the end, teaching about the final judgment.
Means by which God communicated with people such as Joseph, Daniel, the other Joseph, husband of Mary, and the magi. The prophets warn against dreams that do not come from God.
Offering of liquid, usually wine, poured out before God along with sacrifices. Paul uses the image to speak of his life given up: "I am already being poured out as a drink offering".
Jewish wife of the governor Felix, who heard Paul speak of righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come.
Bird of prey, a symbol of strength and protection. The LORD bore Israel "on eagles' wings". Isaiah promises that those who wait for the LORD "will mount up with wings like eagles".
Mountain opposite Gerizim, where Joshua built an altar and read the law on entering Canaan. It was the mountain of curses.
Ethiopian eunuch of the royal household who pleaded with King Zedekiah for the life of Jeremiah, thrown into a cistern.
Book of wisdom attributed to Solomon, which reflects on the meaning of life and ends with the advice: "Fear God and keep his commandments".

Garden that God planted, where he placed the first man and the first woman. Genesis places it "in the east" and mentions four rivers that flowed from it. Its name is associated with delight and gave rise to the expression "paradise".
Region south of the Dead Sea, inhabited by the descendants of Esau. The name is also given to Esau himself.
Country in North Africa, where Abraham took refuge from famine, Joseph was governor and Israel lived as slaves until the exodus. Later the family of Jesus also took refuge there.
Inhabitants of Egypt, where Israel lived as slaves, and where the family of Jesus took refuge.
Judge of the tribe of Benjamin, left-handed, who freed Israel from Eglon, king of Moab, by a cunning act.
Philistine city to which the ark was taken; its population was struck with plague.
Name by which God introduced himself to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, usually translated "God Almighty". The original meaning is disputed.
Region east of Mesopotamia, where the capital Susa stood, which was a Persian royal residence. The story of Esther is set there.

Heads and leaders of a community, who were respected for their experience. In Israel, the elders judged at the gates of the cities. In the church, the presbyters, which in Greek means "elders", were local leaders.
Son of Aaron, who succeeded him as high priest after his father's death on Mount Hor. He helped Joshua distribute the land among the tribes.

God's act of choosing people or a nation for a purpose. Israel was chosen as God's people, and the New Testament speaks of "elect" Christians. Christians differ on how election relates to human freedom.
Priest at Shiloh who raised Samuel. His sons Hophni and Phinehas were unfaithful, and his house suffered the judgment that was announced.
Cry of Jesus on the cross, in Aramaic or Hebrew, quoting Psalm 22. It expresses the pain of his surrender, and the psalm ends in hope.
My God, my God, why have you forsaken me
Servant of Abraham, from Damascus, named as heir before the birth of Isaac. It is also the name of Moses' second son.

Prophet of the northern kingdom who confronted King Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. He was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and Israel expected his return. Jesus linked him with John the Baptist.
Oasis with twelve springs and seventy palm trees, where Israel camped after Marah, on the way to Sinai.
Husband of Naomi, who moved to Moab because of famine in Bethlehem.
Disciple and successor of Elijah, a prophet known for miracles, such as the healing of Naaman and the multiplying of the widow's oil.
Relative of Mary, wife of the priest Zechariah and mother of John the Baptist. In old age she conceived by God's action and greeted Mary as "the mother of my Lord".
Husband of Hannah and father of Samuel, a man of Ramathaim who went up every year to Shiloh to worship. He also had another wife, Peninnah.
Hebrew word for "God" or "gods", plural in form. It is used for the God of Israel from Genesis 1:1.
Jewish sorcerer and false prophet at the court of the proconsul of Cyprus, who opposed Paul and Barnabas and was struck with blindness.
Village near Jerusalem, toward which two disciples were walking when the risen Christ joined them.
Oasis with springs and caves, on the western shore of the Dead Sea, where David hid from Saul and spared him.
City north of Jezreel, where Saul consulted a woman who claimed to be able to speak with the dead, on the eve of his death.
Descendant of Seth who "walked with God" and was taken by him without experiencing death. Hebrews presents him as a man of faith who pleased God.
Pain caused by another's good. Proverbs says that envy is "rottenness of the bones," and Pilate perceived that Jesus had been handed over "for envy." Paul lists it among the works of the flesh.
Co-worker of Paul, a native of Colossae, who taught the churches of the region and prayed earnestly for them.
Messenger of the church of Philippi to Paul in prison, bringing him help. He became gravely ill, but recovered, and Paul sent him back with the letter.
Measure of dry capacity, about 22 liters (about 5 gallons).
Great city of Asia Minor, seat of the worship of Artemis, where Paul stayed for more than two years. The letter to the Ephesians and one of the seven letters of Revelation concern the church there.
Embroidered priestly garment, worn by priests and by the high priest with the breastplate. Sometimes the word refers to an object of worship.
Aramaic word of Jesus when healing a deaf mute, translated: "Be opened."
Second son of Joseph, adopted by Jacob, ancestor of one of the most important tribes. The name "Ephraim" came to designate the northern kingdom.
Sons of Judah, whom God put to death for their wickedness. Onan refused to give offspring to his brother, which led to the episode of Tamar.
Treasurer of the city of Corinth, greeted by Paul in Romans. Another Erastus accompanied Paul in Macedonia.
Isaac's elder son, a hunter, who traded his birthright for a bowl of lentil stew. He is considered the ancestor of the Edomites.
Study of the "last things": the coming of Christ, the resurrection, the judgment and the new world. Christians agree on the central hope but differ on the order and nature of some events.

Jewish group of the time of Jesus that lived in communities devoted to purity and the law, withdrawn from temple life. They are not mentioned in the New Testament. Many scholars associate them with the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Jewish woman who became queen of Persia and risked her life to save her people from Haman's plan of extermination. The feast of Purim recalls the episode.

Life of God, given by faith in Christ, which begins now and is completed in the resurrection. John defines it: "that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you have sent, Jesus Christ".
High official of the queen of the Ethiopians, Candace, who was reading Isaiah on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza. Philip explained the text to him as an announcement of Jesus and baptized him.
Two women of the church at Philippi, who labored with Paul in the gospel. He asks them to be of the same mind in the Lord.
Largest river of western Asia, named among the rivers of Eden and as the boundary of the land promised to Abraham. It ran through Babylon.
Young man of Troas who fell asleep during Paul's long preaching, fell from a window and was lifted up alive.
Proclamation of the good news of Jesus. Jesus sent the disciples to preach to all nations, and the book of Acts shows the gospel spreading from Jerusalem to Rome.
First woman, Adam's companion. Her name is linked to the idea of "life", because she is called "the mother of all the living". With Adam, she is the central figure in the account of the fall.

That which opposes good and God's will. The Bible speaks of moral evil, suffering and spiritual forces, and promises God's final victory. Job and the Psalms deal with the question of the suffering of the righteous.
Encouragement or call to action. Paul lists exhortation among the gifts and urges Christians to encourage one another. The name "Barnabas" means "son of encouragement".
Period in which part of the people of Judah was taken to Babylon, after the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. It ended with the decree of Cyrus.
Departure of Israel from Egypt, under the leadership of Moses. It is the founding event of the people and gives its name to the second book of the Bible.
Priest and prophet in the Babylonian exile, with striking visions, such as the valley of dry bones and the new temple.
Priest and scribe who returned from exile and led the restoration of the Law and of religious life in Judah.
Trust in God and faithfulness to him. Hebrews defines it as "the assurance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen". For Paul, the righteous will live by faith.
Quality of someone who stays firm in his commitments. The Bible exalts the faithfulness of God, who does not change, and calls believers to be faithful. It appears among the fruits of the Spirit.
First city conquered in Canaan: the Israelites marched around the walls for seven days, to the sound of trumpets, and the walls fell. Hebrews praises the faith that made it possible.

Person who speaks in God's name but is not sent by him. The law and the prophets teach how to recognize them, and Jesus warns: "Beware of false prophets". In Revelation, the "false prophet" serves the beast.
Abstaining from food for a time, as a sign of mourning, repentance or seeking God. Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness.
Measure of about 1.8 m, the distance between the hands of a man with arms stretched out. Used by the sailors in Paul's shipwreck.
Reverence before God, which leads to obeying and trusting, and not a fear that drives away. It is called the beginning of wisdom.
Autumn feast in which the Israelites lived in booths for a week, to recall the journey in the wilderness and give thanks for the harvest.
Feast of the first day of the seventh month, marked by the sounding of trumpets, which marks the beginning of the Jewish civil year.
Seven-day feast that accompanies Passover, in which only bread without yeast is eaten, in memory of the haste of the departure from Egypt. Jesus celebrated it with the disciples at the last supper.
Feast of the wheat harvest, seven weeks after Passover, also called Pentecost. It was at this feast that the Spirit was poured out on the disciples in Jerusalem.
Set of annual feasts of Israel prescribed in the law: Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Weeks (Pentecost), Trumpets, Day of Atonement and Tabernacles. Purim and Hanukkah came later.
Miracle in which Jesus fed five thousand people, and on another occasion four thousand, with a few loaves and fish. The first is the only scene of Jesus' ministry reported in all four Gospels.
Roman governor of Judea who heard Paul and kept him in prison for two years, hoping for a bribe.
Sharing life in unity. In the New Testament, the term (koinonia) describes the life of Christians with one another and with God, and also participation in the Lord's Supper.
Felix's successor as governor. Before him, Paul appealed to Caesar.
Episode in which Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to worship the king's statue and were thrown into the furnace, without harm, and the king saw a fourth figure among them.

Tree common in the land of Israel, an image of peace and prosperity. Adam and Eve used fig leaves, and Jesus cursed a fig tree without fruit and taught through the fig tree how to read the signs of the times.
Smallest measure of length, about two centimeters, a quarter of a handbreadth. Jeremiah mentions bronze pillars "four fingers" thick.
In the Bible, a symbol of the presence, purification and judgment of God: the burning bush, the pillar of fire, the tongues of fire at Pentecost. Hebrews says that "our God is a consuming fire".
Letter that speaks of God as light and love, warns against false teachings and gives assurance of eternal life to those who believe.
Letter to scattered Christians who were suffering persecution, with a living hope, a call to holiness and trust in God.
Letter from Paul to the church in Corinth, which answers local problems: divisions, immorality, the Supper, the gifts, love (ch. 13) and the resurrection (ch. 15).
One of the oldest letters of the New Testament. Paul encourages the new church, which was suffering persecution, and speaks of the return of the Lord and of those who died in Christ.
Letter from Paul to Timothy, in Ephesus, about sound teaching, prayer, requirements for overseers and deacons and personal conduct.

First male child or first male offspring of an animal, which belonged to God. The firstborn of Israel were spared at the Passover, and were "redeemed". Jesus is called "firstborn of all creation" and "firstborn from the dead".
First produce of the harvest or the flock, offered to God in recognition. Paul calls Christ the "first fruits of those who are asleep", for having been the first to rise.
Common food in the Sea of Galilee. Several disciples were fishermen, and Jesus called them to be "fishers of men". The fish also appears in the miracles of multiplication and of the catch.

In the Bible, the word can mean the physical body, the frail human condition or, in Paul, the human nature inclined to sin, as opposed to the Spirit. John uses "flesh" to speak of the incarnation of the Word.
Episode in which Joseph, warned in a dream, took Mary and the child to Egypt to escape from Herod, who had the boys of Bethlehem killed. After the return, the family settled in Nazareth.
Universal or regional flood sent by God because of humanity's violence. Noah and his family were saved in the ark.
Wind instrument used at feasts and funerals. Jesus compares the generation to children who play the flute, but nobody dances.
Gesture of Jesus on the night before his death: he washed the disciples' feet as a humble service, telling them to do the same for one another.

Person who lives among a people who are not his own. Israel's law commands loving and protecting the foreigner, "for you were strangers in the land of Egypt". In the New Testament, Christians are called pilgrims and strangers.
Act of God that removes the guilt of sin, and act of the human being who stops demanding payment for an offense. Jesus taught that the disciples must forgive as they have been forgiven.
The four horsemen of the Apocalypse, who accompany the first four seals: a white horse, a red one, a black one and a pale one, associated with conquest, war, famine and death.
Animal of cunning appearance. Jesus said: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head".
Condition of one who is not bound. Israel was set free from Egypt. For Paul, Christ set us free from sin and from the law as a way of justification, but freedom must serve love.
Qualities that the Spirit produces in those who are faithful to him: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control.
Angel sent to Daniel, to Zechariah and to Mary to announce important messages from God, such as the birth of John the Baptist and of Jesus.
Seventh son of Jacob, first of Zilpah, and the tribe that settled east of the Jordan, in the region of Gilead.
Prophet and seer who accompanied David, advised him in the time when he was fleeing from Saul and brought him the word of the Lord after the census.
Region east of the Sea of Galilee where Jesus set free a man possessed by a legion of demons, who entered a herd of pigs.
Name of several Christians of the New Testament, among them Paul's host in Corinth and the recipient of John's third letter.
Region of Asia Minor, where Paul founded churches and to which he wrote a letter.
Region of northern Israel, around the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus spent most of his ministry.

Proconsul of Achaia who refused to judge the accusation against Paul in Corinth, treating it as an internal Jewish matter. An inscription from Delphi that mentions him helps date Paul's stay in Corinth.
Pharisee and respected teacher of the Law, who advised the Sanhedrin to be cautious with the apostles. Paul says he was his student.
Philistine city, home of Goliath and where David fled from Saul. Later it became part of David's domain.
One of the five cities of the Philistines, on the coast. Samson was imprisoned there and there he brought down the temple of Dagon. Philip met the Ethiopian eunuch on the road to Gaza.
Governor of Judah appointed by Nebuchadnezzar after the fall of Jerusalem. He was assassinated by Ishmael, which led many to flee to Egypt.
Servant of Elisha who, out of greed, ran after Naaman to receive payment and was struck with leprosy.

Word of Hebrew origin ("valley of Hinnom"), referring to a valley near Jerusalem, used as an image of judgment and destruction. Translations often render it "hell". Its meaning and the nature of the punishment are debated among Christians.
Set of seven New Testament letters addressed to Christians in general: James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2 and 3 John and Jude.
First book of the Bible, whose name means "origin". It tells the creation, the fall, the flood, Babel and the story of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
Person who is not Jewish. The message of Jesus was extended to the Gentiles, especially through the ministry of Paul.
Philistine city in southern Canaan, where Abraham and Isaac lived as foreigners and dealt with King Abimelech.
Mountain near Shechem, sacred to the Samaritans, who had their temple there. It was the mountain of blessing at Israel's entry into Canaan.
Sons of Moses and Zipporah, born in Midian. The name Gershom recalls "a stranger in a foreign land."
Garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives, where Jesus prayed in anguish on the night he was arrested. Its name means "oil press".
City of Benjamin, home of Saul and capital of his kingdom. A place of crime and civil war in the days of the judges.
City whose inhabitants deceived Joshua to make a covenant with Israel. There Solomon offered sacrifices and asked for wisdom.
Inhabitants of Gibeon who, by cunning, made an alliance with Joshua. They were spared and came to serve in the sanctuary as woodcutters and water carriers.
Judge of Israel who, with only three hundred men, defeated the Midianites. Before the battle he asked God for a sign with a fleece of wool.
Mountain where Saul and Jonathan died in the battle against the Philistines. David mourned their death there.
Mountainous region east of the Jordan, famous for its balm, where Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh settled.
Place of Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan, where Samuel and Saul had important moments.
One of the peoples of Canaan named in the promise to Abraham and in the conquest of the land.
Custom of the law of leaving the forgotten ears of grain and the corners of the field for the poor and the foreigners. Ruth gleaned in the fields of Boaz.
In the Bible, the weight and radiance of God's presence, and also the honor due to him. The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle and the temple. John says that in Jesus "we saw his glory".
Flock animal. In the law, a goat was sacrificed on the Day of Atonement. In Matthew 25, the goats represent those who are separated at the judgment.

Creator of all things and Lord of Israel. In the Bible he appears with many names, such as Elohim, El Shaddai and the holy four-letter name, YHWH. Christians confess him as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel and attended the synagogue, without having become full proselytes. Cornelius is an example. Many of them believed Paul's message.

Precious metal, used in the tabernacle, in the temple and in jewelry. In the Bible, it is also an image of what is valuable and goes through the fire. Peter says that tested faith is more precious than gold.
Idol that Aaron made at the request of the people while Moses was on Mount Sinai. Moses, when he came down, broke the tablets of the law and interceded for the people.
Principle taught by Jesus: "Whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them". Jesus says that it sums up the Law and the Prophets.
Place outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. Its Aramaic name means "place of the skull", and the Latin form is Calvary.
Philistine giant from Gath who challenged the army of Israel and was defeated by David with a sling and a stone.
Woman whom the prophet Hosea married by the Lord's command, as an image of God's love for an unfaithful people.
Translation of the word "gospel". To announce good news is to announce the salvation and the Kingdom of God, proclaimed by Jesus.
Parable in answer to the question "who is my neighbor?". A Samaritan cares for a wounded man whom a priest and a Levite had left. Jesus concludes: "Go and do likewise".
Fertile region of the Nile delta, in Egypt, where Jacob's family settled and lived until the exodus.
Word meaning "good news". In the writings of the New Testament it is the message about Jesus Christ. It also names the four books that tell of his life: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
Gospel that presents Jesus as the Word made flesh, through seven "signs" and the "I am" discourses. It was written "that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God".

Gospel that Luke, companion of Paul, wrote to Theophilus. It highlights the poor, women, sinners and joy. It includes the parables of the good Samaritan and of the prodigal son. It is the first part of a work that continues in Acts.
Shortest Gospel and, according to many scholars, the first to be written. It tells of the action and the passion of Jesus, the Son of God who serves and suffers, at a fast pace.

First Gospel of the New Testament, written for readers with a strong Jewish background, which shows Jesus as the promised Messiah, Son of David, and gathers five great discourses, among them the Sermon on the Mount.
Undeserved favor of God, given out of love and without merit on the part of the one who receives it. It is a central theme of Paul's letters, as in "by grace you have been saved".
Parables about a banquet for which the guests make excuses, and the poor and the foreigners are called in their place. It portrays the Kingdom and the response to God's invitation.
Command of the risen Christ to the disciples: to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to observe what he commanded, with the promise "I am with you always".

Jesus' answer to the question about the greatest commandment: to love the Lord with all one's heart, soul and mind, and to love one's neighbor as oneself. On these depend all the Law and the Prophets.
People of Greek language and culture, dominant in the Mediterranean after Alexander. The New Testament was written in Greek, and "Greek" also designated, in general, non-Jews.
Prophet who questioned God about injustice and received the answer that "the righteous shall live by his faith".
Edomite prince who fled to Egypt as a child and, after the death of David, returned as an adversary of Solomon.
King of Zobah, defeated by David, together with the Arameans who supported him.

Greek word for the place of the dead, equivalent to the Hebrew Sheol. Jesus says that the gates of Hades will not prevail against the church, and Revelation says that Hades is thrown into the lake of fire.
Egyptian servant of Sarah, who became Abraham's concubine and the mother of Ishmael. When she fled, God visited her in the desert and heard her distress.
Prophet of the post-exile period who urged the people to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.
Hebrew expression of praise meaning "praise the Lord". It appears in the Psalms and in Revelation.
Son of Noah, presented as the father of Cush, Mizraim (Egypt), Put and Canaan. His episode with his father's drunkenness resulted in the curse on Canaan, his son.
High official of King Ahasuerus who planned to exterminate the Jews in the Persian empire, but was hanged on the gallows prepared for Mordecai.
Hamor, a Hivite prince, and his son Shechem. Shechem violated Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, and wanted to marry her. The sons of Jacob took revenge, killing the men of the city.
False prophet of Jeremiah's time, who announced the near end of the Babylonian yoke and broke the wooden yoke that Jeremiah wore on his neck. Jeremiah told him he would die that year, and so it was.

Mother of Samuel (another Anna, the elderly prophetess of the temple, appears in Luke 2), who, being childless, prayed at the sanctuary of Shiloh and dedicated her son to God. Her song of thanksgiving inspired Mary's Magnificat.
Jewish festival of lights, which recalls the purification of the temple in the time of the Maccabees. John calls it the Feast of the Dedication.
King of the Ammonites who humiliated David's messengers, which provoked a war.
City in northern Mesopotamia where Abraham stayed for a time and where Jacob lived with Laban.
Stringed instruments used in worship and in daily life. David played the harp to calm Saul, and the psalms invite us to praise the LORD with harp and lyre.
Time of gathering what was planted, an image of the final judgment and of mission. Jesus says: "The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few".
King of Aram (Syria). Elijah was sent to anoint him, and Elisha foresaw the cruelty of his reign against Israel.
Important city-state of northern Canaan, taken and burned by Joshua. Later it was fortified by Solomon.
In the Bible, the center of the person: thought, will and affection, more than just feelings. "Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life."
In the Bible, it designates both the sky and the place of God's presence. The Lord's Prayer begins "Our Father in heaven", and Revelation speaks of "a new heaven and a new earth".
Oldest name for the descendants of Abraham, used mostly by foreigners. The letter to the Hebrews was addressed to Christians of Jewish origin.

Lunar calendar of twelve months, adjusted by the occasional addition of a month, used in Israel. The religious year begins in Nisan (March–April), the month of Passover; the civil year, in Tishri. Days begin at sunset.
City of Judah, where Abraham settled and was buried with Sarah in the cave of Machpelah. It was David's first capital.
Word used in English to translate different terms: "Sheol" or "Hades", the place of the dead, and "Gehenna", an image of the final judgment. Christians differ on its nature and duration.
Jews of Greek language and culture. In Acts, the Hellenists of the Jerusalem church complained about the treatment of their widows, and from this the seven were chosen.
From the Greek for "choice", it came to name a teaching that departs from the received faith. The New Testament warns against false teachers and "destructive heresies".
Highest mountain of northern Israel, covered with snow, from which springs of the Jordan rise. Some see in it the mountain of the transfiguration.
Name of two descendants of Herod. Agrippa I had James killed and Peter arrested; Agrippa II heard Paul's defense.
Son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee, who had John the Baptist arrested and killed and before whom Jesus was brought before being handed over to Pilate.
King of Judea at the time of Jesus' birth, who ordered the massacre of the boys of Bethlehem and rebuilt the temple of Jerusalem.
Supporters of the dynasty of Herod, who joined the Pharisees to try to trap Jesus with a question about the tax.

Wife of Herod Antipas, previously married to a half-brother of his. John the Baptist censured this marriage and, through her scheming, was imprisoned and beheaded. The daughter who asked for John's head is called Salome by the historian Josephus.
King of Judah who reformed worship, trusted in God when the Assyrian king Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem, and had his life extended after a serious illness.
Two short parables in which someone sells everything to obtain a treasure in a field or a valuable pearl, to teach the supreme value of the Kingdom of God.

Chief of the priests, the only one who entered the most holy place once a year, on the Day of Atonement. In Jesus' time his office carried great political power. Hebrews presents Jesus as the perfect high priest.

Name given to the prayer of Jesus in John 17, on the night before his arrest, in which he asks for the glory of the Father, for the protection and sanctification of the disciples and for the unity of all who would believe.
High priest in the reign of Josiah, who found the book of the law in the temple.
Hebrew measure for liquids, about 3.6 liters (about 1 gallon).
Valley south of Jerusalem where, in times of idolatry, children were burned to Molech. From it comes the image of Gehenna, the place of judgment.
King of Tyre, friend of David and Solomon, who sent cedar wood and craftsmen for David's palace and for the temple.
Books of the Old Testament that tell the history of Israel: Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings, 1 and 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah and Esther.
People who lived in Canaan and in Anatolia. Uriah, soldier of David, was a Hittite.
People of Canaan. The Gibeonites were Hivites and deceived Joshua in order to make peace with Israel.
Quality of God that sets him apart from all things. People, places and objects are "holy" when set apart for him. The Bible calls God's people to be holy because he is holy.
First room of the tabernacle and of the temple, where the lampstand, the table of the bread of the Presence and the altar of incense stood. Only the priests entered there.

Presence and power of God at work. In the Old Testament it is the breath that gives life and empowers prophets; in the New Testament it is promised by Jesus and received by the disciples at Pentecost. John calls him the Counselor or Paraclete.
Dry measure of about 220 liters, equal to ten ephahs. The cor has the same value. The parable of the unjust steward mentions a hundred cors of wheat.
Natural sweetener, a symbol of abundance. Canaan is called a land "flowing with milk and honey". John the Baptist ate locusts and wild honey.
Confident expectation in God's promises, above all in the resurrection and the final restoration. Together with faith and love, it forms the central trio of the New Testament.
Sons of the priest Eli at Shiloh, who abused their office. They died in the battle against the Philistines on the day the ark was taken, and the news killed their father.
Another name for Mount Sinai or a neighboring mountain, "the mountain of God", where Moses saw the bush and Israel received the law.
Ancient inhabitants of Seir, whom the Edomites, descendants of Esau, drove out.
War animal, a symbol of military power. The Bible warns against trusting in horses and chariots instead of God. It appears in visions, such as the horsemen of Revelation.
Cry of praise and plea meaning "save, please". The crowd shouted it when Jesus entered Jerusalem.
Prophet of the northern kingdom, who lived out his marriage to Gomer as an image of God's love for unfaithful Israel.
Last king of Israel, who rebelled against Assyria. Samaria was besieged and the northern kingdom came to an end.
The Jews counted the hours of the day from sunrise. "The third hour" corresponds to about nine in the morning, "the sixth" to noon, and "the ninth" to three in the afternoon.
Parable that closes the Sermon on the Mount: whoever hears the words of Jesus and does them is like the man who builds his house on the rock, which withstands the storm.
Prophetess of Jerusalem, consulted by King Josiah about the book of the law found in the temple. She confirmed the judgment on the city, but promised peace to the king.

Recognition that everything depends on God and willingness to serve. Jesus describes himself as "gentle and lowly in heart", and Paul urges having the same mind that was in Christ, who humbled himself.
Companion of Moses and Aaron. With Aaron he held up Moses' arms in the battle against Amalek and was left in charge of the people when Moses went up Sinai.
Friend and counselor of David who pretended to join Absalom in order to frustrate Ahithophel's counsel, giving David time to flee.
False teachers who, according to the letters to Timothy, made shipwreck of the faith. They said that the resurrection had already happened.
Appearance of piety without the reality. Jesus condemns it in Pharisees and scribes who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from him.
Plant of small branches used in purification rites to sprinkle blood or water. The psalmist asks: "Purify me with hyssop".

Declarations of Jesus in the Gospel of John: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, and the true vine. They echo the divine name revealed to Moses.
City of Galatia, visited by Paul and Barnabas on the first journey.
Worship of idols, or of anything put in the place of God. The first and second commandments forbid it, and Paul says that greed is also idolatry.
Region south of Judah where the Edomites lived. Herod the Great came from an Idumean family.
Genesis teaches that human beings were created "in the image and likeness" of God, which gives them dignity and responsibility. The New Testament calls Christ the "image of the invisible God".
Name that means "God with us". Isaiah applies it to a child who was a sign, and Matthew applies it to Jesus.
Condition of one who does not die. The Bible says that God alone has immortality by nature, and promises believers eternal life and an incorruptible body in the resurrection.
Christian belief that the Son of God became human in Jesus. John says that "the Word became flesh and lived among us".
Aromatic resin burned in worship, as a symbol of prayers. One of the gifts of the magi to Jesus. It was burned daily on the altar of the tabernacle and of the temple.
Word used to say that the Scriptures come from God. Paul says that "all Scripture is God-breathed" (literally, "breathed out by God"), useful for teaching, reproof and correction.
Prayer on behalf of others. Abraham intercedes for Sodom, Moses for the people; the New Testament says that Christ and the Spirit intercede for us and that Christians should pray for one another.
Strong metal, used in weapons and tools. The Canaanites had chariots of iron. Psalm 2 and Revelation speak of a "rod of iron".

Son of the promise to Abraham and Sarah, father of Esau and Jacob. The account of his near-sacrifice on Mount Moriah, stopped by God, is one of the best-remembered stories of Genesis. His name means "he laughs".

Prophet of Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, author of the book that bears his name. His prophecies of the suffering Servant and of Immanuel are widely quoted in the New Testament. He was called by God in a vision in the temple.
Son of Saul, proclaimed king over Israel by Abner after his father's death, while David reigned in Judah. He was assassinated, and David became king of all the people.
Son of Abraham and Hagar. God promised to make him a great nation. Tradition considers him an ancestor of Arab peoples.
Descendants of Ishmael, desert merchants who carried spices to Egypt. They were the ones who bought Joseph from his brothers.

Name given to Jacob after wrestling with God at Peniel, it came to designate his descendants, the people of God. After the division of the kingdom, "Israel" came to name especially the northern kingdom, with its capital in Samaria, in contrast with Judah. In the New Testament, "Israel" also appears as the people of the covenant in a broad sense.
Descendant of Jacob, also called Israel. The name came to designate the people, the northern kingdom and, in the New Testament, the people of God.
Ninth son of Jacob, fifth of Leah. The tribe settled in the fertile plain of Jezreel, and Jacob compares him to a strong donkey that submits to labor.
Region northeast of Galilee, ruled by Philip during the ministry of John the Baptist.

Sons of Lamech, in the genealogy of Cain. Jabal was the father of those who live in tents and raise livestock; Jubal, the father of those who play the harp and flute; Tubal Cain, the forger of instruments of bronze and iron. They show the beginning of the arts and trades.
Stream east of the Jordan where Jacob wrestled with God on the eve of meeting Esau.
Man of Judah "more honorable than his brothers", whose prayer for blessing and protection was granted by God.

Son of Isaac, father of the twelve patriarchs of the tribes of Israel. After wrestling with a divine being at Peniel, he received the name Israel, "he who struggles with God". His dream of the ladder at Bethel is one of the best-known episodes.
Kenite woman who welcomed the commander Sisera into her tent and killed him with a tent peg, fulfilling what Deborah had said: that the Lord would hand him over to a woman.
Ruler of a synagogue whose twelve-year-old daughter Jesus raised after he asked for help.
Fisherman, brother of John and son of Zebedee, one of the twelve apostles and among those closest to Jesus. He was the first apostle to be martyred, executed by order of Herod Agrippa I.
One of the twelve apostles, sometimes identified as "James the Less". Little is said of him in the gospels.
James the brother of the Lord
Brother of Jesus who, after the resurrection, became a leader of the church in Jerusalem. Tradition attributes to him the letter of James.
Son of Noah, ancestor of peoples who spread along the coasts and islands to the north and west, according to the table of nations in Genesis.
Canaanite people who lived in Jebus, the future Jerusalem. Only in the time of David was the city taken.
Son of Josiah, king of Judah for only three months, deposed by Pharaoh Neco and taken to Egypt.
King of Judah, son of Jehoiakim, taken captive to Babylon with the elite of the people in 597 BC. Thirty-seven years later he was released from prison and received a place at the king's table.
High priest in the time of Athaliah, who hid the boy Joash, crowned him king at seven years old and led the renewal of the covenant.
King of Judah, son of Josiah, who cut up and burned the scroll of Jeremiah's words and rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar.
King of Judah, son of Asa, who sought the Lord, sent teachers to teach the law through the cities and reorganized justice. He imprudently allied himself with Ahab.
Commander anointed by Elisha's order to be king of Israel. He wiped out the house of Ahab, Jezebel and the worshipers of Baal, but did not abandon the calves of Jeroboam.
Judge of Israel who made a hard vow before fighting the Ammonites.
Prophet of Judah before and during the fall of Jerusalem, known as the "weeping prophet". He announced the exile and the new covenant written on hearts.
City near the Jordan, one of the oldest in the world, whose walls fell in the time of Joshua. Jesus healed the blind Bartimaeus and visited Zacchaeus there.
First king of the northern kingdom, Israel, after the division. To keep the people from going to Jerusalem, he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan.

Capital of David's kingdom and site of the temple. It is called the "city of David" and "Zion". City where Jesus was crucified and where the church was born. In the Bible it becomes a symbol of God's presence and of final hope, the "heavenly Jerusalem".
