High priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and led the rebuilding of the altar and the temple. Zechariah sees him in a vision, cleansed before the Lord.
Father of David, of Bethlehem, of the tribe of Judah. Samuel went to his house to anoint one of his sons, and Isaiah announces a "shoot from the stump of Jesse".

Center of the New Testament. Born in Bethlehem and raised in Nazareth, he preached the Kingdom of God, taught in parables, healed the sick, was crucified under Pontius Pilate and, according to the Gospels, rose on the third day. Christians confess him as Messiah and Lord. His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, "the Lord saves".
Priest of Midian and father-in-law of Moses, who advised him to delegate justice in the desert.
Originally, an inhabitant of the kingdom of Judah. After the exile it designates the Hebrew people as a whole.
Queen of Israel, wife of Ahab, who spread the worship of Baal and persecuted the prophets of God. Her name became a byword for wickedness.
Fertile valley and city of the north. There stood Naboth's vineyard and Ahab's palace, and there Jezebel died.
Commander of David's army, a loyal and violent soldier, the king's nephew.
Wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, who followed Jesus and helped him with her means. She was among the women who went to the tomb.
King of Judah who came to the throne at seven years old, protected by the priest Jehoiada.

Upright man of Uz, who lost his possessions, children and health and debated with his friends about the meaning of suffering. God answered him out of a whirlwind. He is remembered as an example of perseverance.

Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, came to comfort Job and ended up arguing that suffering is always punishment for sin. God rebuked them for not having spoken rightly about him. Elihu, who was younger, speaks after them.
Mother of Moses, Aaron and Miriam, of the tribe of Levi. She hid her newborn son and put him in a basket by the Nile.
Prophet who announced a plague of locusts as a sign of "the day of the Lord" and promised the outpouring of the Spirit, which Peter cited at Pentecost.
Fisherman, brother of James and son of Zebedee, one of the twelve apostles, called "the disciple whom Jesus loved". Tradition attributes to him the fourth gospel, three letters and Revelation.

Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, a prophet who preached in the Judean wilderness a baptism of repentance and prepared the way for Jesus, whom he baptized in the Jordan. He was imprisoned and beheaded by order of Herod Antipas.
Prophet sent to Nineveh, who first fled from God, was swallowed by a great fish and then preached to the city. Jesus cited him as a sign of his resurrection.
Son of Saul and faithful friend of David. Although heir to the throne, he recognized that David would be king and protected him from his father's anger.
Mediterranean port city. Jonah embarked from there; Peter stayed there in the house of Simon the tanner, where he had the vision that led him to Cornelius.
Name of two contemporary kings: Joram of Israel, son of Ahab, and Jehoram of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat and married to a daughter of Ahab. Both turned away from the Lord.
Principal river of Israel, flowing from Mount Hermon to the Dead Sea. Joshua crossed it on entering Canaan, and in it Jesus was baptized.

Son of Jacob and Rachel, sold by his brothers as a slave in Egypt. He became governor after interpreting Pharaoh's dreams and saved his family from famine, forgiving his brothers. His sons Ephraim and Manasseh gave their names to tribes of Israel.
Wealthy member of the Sanhedrin and secret disciple of Jesus, who asked Pilate for the Lord's body and placed it in his own new tomb.

Carpenter of Nazareth, husband of Mary and adoptive father of Jesus, a descendant of David. Matthew describes him as a righteous man, warned in dreams to protect his family, including in the flight to Egypt.
Assistant and successor of Moses, who led Israel into Canaan, from the crossing of the Jordan to the division of the land. His name is the Hebrew form of the name "Jesus".
King of Judah who rediscovered the book of the Law in the temple and led a deep religious reform. He became king as a boy and died in battle against Egypt.
King of Judah, son of Uzziah, who reigned uprightly and strengthened the kingdom.
Special year, every fifty years, in which lands returned to their original owners and Hebrew slaves were set free. Jesus applied to his mission the language of the "acceptable year of the Lord".

Fourth son of Jacob and Leah, from whom the tribe of Judah descends, and later King David and, according to the New Testament, Jesus. The southern kingdom, with its capital in Jerusalem, took his name.
Christians, generally Jews, who held that Gentiles had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. Paul fought them in the letter to the Galatians.
One of the twelve apostles, treasurer of the group, who handed Jesus over to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. Afterward, filled with remorse, he died.
Author, according to tradition, of the short letter of Jude, which urges believers to contend for the faith handed down to the saints.
Region of southern Palestine, centered on Jerusalem, governed in Jesus' time by Roman prefects.

Leaders raised up by God to deliver Israel from oppressors in the time between Joshua and the kings, such as Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. It also names the biblical book that tells this period.
God's judgment on human beings and nations. In the Bible it is both a reason for fear and a hope for the oppressed.

Dispute between two women over the same child, which Solomon resolved by proposing to divide the baby in two. The true mother revealed herself by preferring to give up her son. The episode illustrated the wisdom of the king.
Centurion of the imperial cohort who took Paul prisoner to Rome. He treated him kindly and spared him in the storm and the shipwreck.

God's declaration that welcomes someone as righteous. For Paul, it happens through faith in Christ and not by works of the Law. James insists that true faith shows itself in actions. The relationship between the two texts is debated by the different Christian traditions.
Oasis south of Canaan where Israel stayed a long time, from which the spies were sent and where Miriam died.
People linked to Midian, who lived in the southern desert. Jethro and Jael were Kenites. Some Kenites joined the Israelites.
Woman whom Abraham took after Sarah's death. She had six sons, among them Midian, ancestor of the Midianites.
Valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. David crossed it fleeing from Absalom, and Jesus crossed it with the disciples on the way to Gethsemane.

Ruler of a kingdom. Israel asked for a king "like the nations", and God gave them Saul and then David. The law regulates the role of the king, and the Bible speaks of God as King and of the Messiah as the promised king.

Central theme of Jesus' preaching: God's reign that draws near and shows itself in his person. Matthew uses the form "kingdom of heaven". It is presented as present and, at the same time, still to be fulfilled.
City where the ark of the covenant stayed for twenty years after returning from the Philistines, until David took it to Jerusalem.

Levite who, with Dathan and Abiram, rebelled against Moses and Aaron in the name of the equality of all the people. The earth opened and swallowed them. The sons of Korah continued to serve in worship, and several psalms bear the name "of the sons of Korah".
Brother of Rebekah and father-in-law of Jacob, who deceived him and made him work years for Leah and Rachel.
Image of the final judgment in Revelation, called the "second death", into which are thrown death, Hades, the devil and those not found in the book of life.
Title given to Jesus by John the Baptist, tied to the Passover lamb and to Isaiah's suffering servant. In Revelation, the Lamb is worthy to open the book and to receive praise.
Name of two descendants before the flood: one of the line of Cain, a violent poet, and another of that of Seth, father of Noah.
Book of five poems of mourning for the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah.
Seven-branched gold lampstand, in the holy place of the tabernacle, whose lamps were to burn continually. It is a symbol of Judaism.
City in Asia, near Colossae, seat of one of the seven churches of Revelation, rebuked for being "lukewarm". Colossians mentions a letter sent to it.
Belief that, at the end, God will judge all people. Jesus speaks of the separation of the sheep from the goats, and Revelation describes the judgment before the great white throne.

In the strict sense, the first five books of the Bible, or the set of commandments given to Israel through Moses. The Hebrew word "Torah" means "instruction". Jesus affirmed that he did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it.
Gesture of placing hands on someone to bless, heal, commission or transmit the Spirit. Moses did it with Joshua; the apostles, with the seven deacons; the church of Antioch, with Barnabas and Saul.
Brother of Martha and Mary of Bethany, a friend of Jesus, who raised him after four days in the tomb. He should not be confused with the Lazarus of the parable of the rich man.
First wife of Jacob, daughter of Laban, mother of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun and Dinah. Jacob was led to marry her before Rachel.
Small portion that makes the whole dough rise. Jesus uses it in the parable of the Kingdom. In other passages, "leaven" is an image of corruption, like the leaven of the Pharisees.
Mountainous region north of Israel, famous for its cedars, which Solomon used in the temple.
Name given by a demon-possessed man of Gerasa, who said he was "many". Jesus freed him, and the spirits entered pigs.

In the Bible, the word translates a group of skin diseases. The law ordered the leper to live outside the camp and to proclaim himself unclean. Jesus touched and healed lepers, restoring them to community life.
Letter of practical guidance: faith that shows itself in works, control of the tongue, patience, prayer and care for the poor.
Short letter that warns against false teachers and calls to faithfulness, citing examples from the Old Testament and a prophecy of Enoch. It ends with a beautiful doxology.
Letter that proclaims the supremacy of Christ over all creation and warns against false teachings.
Letter about the church as the body of Christ, the unity of Jews and Gentiles, salvation by grace and the "armor of God".
Letter that defends the gospel of grace against the demand for circumcision for the Gentiles: justification is by faith in Christ, and life in the Spirit produces fruit.

Anonymous letter, addressed to Christians of Jewish origin, which presents Christ as superior to the angels, to Moses and to the Levitical priesthood. It includes the "gallery of faith" of chapter 11.
Letter of gratitude and joy, written by Paul in prison, which includes the hymn to Christ who humbled himself to the point of the cross.

Letter from Paul to the church in Rome, written around AD 56-57, which expounds the gospel: all have sinned, righteousness comes by faith in Christ, life in the Spirit, the place of Israel and the Christian life.
Letter from Paul to Titus about the organization of the churches of Crete, the choice of elders and the Christian life consistent with grace.
Third son of Jacob and Leah, ancestor of the priestly tribe. The Levites received no land, and served in the sanctuary.
Creatures described in God's speeches to Job as images of the power of creation that only God masters. In the prophets and in the Psalms, Leviathan represents the chaos and evil that God will defeat.
Custom of the law by which the brother of a man who died childless married the widow, so that the dead man's name would not be lost. It appears in the stories of Tamar and of Ruth.
Member of the tribe of Levi, dedicated to the service of the tabernacle and the temple, assisting the priests, teaching the Law and leading the music.
Third book of the Bible, about the worship and holiness of Israel: the sacrifices, the priesthood, the rules of purity, the Day of Atonement and the call "be holy, for I am holy".
Lack of truth in word or action. The law forbids false witness, and Proverbs says that lying lips are an abomination to the LORD. Jesus calls the devil the "father of lies."
Symbol of revelation, life and the presence of God. Jesus said he was "the light of the world" and called the disciples "the light of the world".

Jesus calls the disciples the "salt of the earth" and the "light of the world", images of their role in society. The light is not hidden under a basket, but shines so that people may see the good works and glorify the Father.
Flower of the field, recalled by Jesus to teach trust in God's care: "Consider the lilies of the field". The Song of Solomon uses the lily as an image of beauty.
Plant fiber used to make fabrics. Fine linen was used in the garments of the priests and in the curtains of the tabernacle. In Revelation, "the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints".

Animal symbol of strength and royalty. Jacob calls Judah a "lion". David and Daniel faced lions, Peter compares the devil to a roaring lion, and Revelation calls Christ the "Lion of the tribe of Judah".
Episode in which Daniel, for praying to God despite the king's prohibition, was thrown to the lions, and God kept him safe. Darius then proclaimed faith in the God of Daniel.

Running water, as opposed to still water. Jesus offers himself as a source of "living water" to the Samaritan woman and, in the temple, invites the thirsty to come to him. Jeremiah says that the people abandoned the "spring of living waters".
Insect that, in swarms, devastates crops. It was one of the plagues of Egypt, and Joel uses the image of the invasion of locusts. John the Baptist ate them.
Small liquid measure, a little over three tenths of a liter, used in the purification rites of the leper.
Title of Christ in John 1: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God". In Greek, Logos. Christians understand him as the Word of God who became flesh in Jesus.
Patience in the face of offenses. It appears among the fruits of the Spirit. Peter says that the Lord is not slow about his promise, but is patient, wanting all to repent.

In English, the divine name revealed to Moses (the four Hebrew letters YHWH) is usually translated "LORD", in capitals. The Jews avoided pronouncing it and read "Adonai", "Lord". In the New Testament, "Lord" is a title of Jesus.
Prayer taught by Jesus, recorded in Matthew and in Luke, which begins "Our Father in heaven".
Meal of bread and wine instituted by Jesus at the last supper, in memory of his death. Paul passes on the words of institution, and the churches celebrate it with different interpretations.
Parable of the woman who lights the lamp and searches for the lost coin until she finds it, and invites her neighbors to rejoice.
Parable of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to look for the straying sheep and celebrates when he finds it, an image of the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
Abraham's nephew, who separated from him and went to live in the region of Sodom. He was led out of the city before its destruction, but his wife looked back and became a pillar of salt.

In Greek, the selfless love that God has for human beings and that they should have for God and for their neighbor. The greatest commandment, according to Jesus, sums up the Law: to love God and neighbor.
Physician and companion of Paul, to whom tradition attributes the gospel that bears his name and the book of Acts. The passages of Acts written in "we" indicate his presence on Paul's journeys.
City near Joppa, where Peter healed Aeneas, paralyzed for eight years, which led many to believe.
Dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, in Philippi, who welcomed Paul and was the first convert in Europe.
City of Lycaonia where Paul healed a cripple and the people wanted to worship them as gods. Shortly afterward, Paul was stoned there. It was also the home of Timothy.

Jewish family led by Judas Maccabeus who, in the 2nd century BC, led the revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus Epiphanes. They restored the temple, an event remembered at Hanukkah. Their books are among the deuterocanonical.
Region of northern Greece, to which Paul was called in a vision, after which he founded churches in Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea.
Cave near Hebron, bought by Abraham for the burial of Sarah. Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah were also buried there.
City on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, home of Mary Magdalene.

Wise men from the east who, guided by a star, came to Jerusalem and to Bethlehem to worship the child Jesus and offered him gold, frankincense and myrrh. The Bible does not say that there were three or that they were kings; that comes from later tradition.
Song of praise by Mary at the visit to Elizabeth, which celebrates God's mercy toward the humble and echoes the song of Hannah.
In Ezekiel, Gog is the chief of Magog, a northern power that attacks Israel. In Revelation, they are nations at war against God's people at the end.

The prophetic books of the Old Testament. The major ones (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel and Daniel) are longer. The twelve minor ones, from Hosea to Malachi, are shorter, not less important.
Prophet whose book closes the Old Testament, who announced a messenger who would prepare the way of the Lord.
Servant of the high priest whose ear Peter cut off in Gethsemane. Luke tells that Jesus healed him. Only John gives the name.
Island in the Mediterranean where Paul was shipwrecked on his way to Rome and was welcomed, staying three months.
Word of Aramaic origin for wealth. Jesus said that no one can serve God and Mammon.
Place near Hebron, with a grove of oaks, where Abraham pitched his tent and received the visit of the three men who announced the birth of Isaac.
Eldest son of Joseph, ancestor of one of the tribes of Israel. Also the name of a king of Judah, with a long and evil reign.

Son of Hezekiah and king of Judah for fifty-five years, the longest reign, marked by idolatry and violence. According to Chronicles, he was taken captive to Babylon and there humbled himself before God.
Plant with a thick root, believed to promote fertility. Rachel and Leah quarreled over mandrakes that Reuben brought from the field.
Food that God gave the people in the wilderness for forty years. The word means "What is it?". Jesus called himself the "bread of life", in contrast with manna.
Foods that God gave the Israelites in the wilderness: manna in the morning and quail in the evening.
Father of Samson, to whom the angel of the Lord announced the birth of his son.
Aramaic expression that Paul uses at the end of a letter, understood as "come, Lord" or "the Lord comes". It was a prayer and confession of the early church.
Co-worker of Peter, Barnabas and Paul, to whom tradition attributes the second gospel. He left the first missionary journey, but was later considered useful by Paul.
Sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany, who received Jesus in her house and made the confession "I believe that you are the Christ".
From the Greek "witness". One who gives his life because of his faith. Stephen is remembered as the first Christian martyr.

Young woman of Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, who received from the angel Gabriel the announcement that she would be the mother of Jesus. She is present at his birth, at Cana, at the cross and among the disciples gathered after the ascension. Her song of praise is known as the Magnificat.
Follower of Jesus from whom he cast out seven demons. She was at the crucifixion and was the first to see the risen Christ, being sent to announce the news to the disciples.
Sister of Martha and Lazarus, who sat at the feet of Jesus to listen to him and anointed his feet with costly perfume.
One of the women present at the cross of Jesus and at the tomb. She may be the same Mary the mother of James and Joseph.
Woman of Jerusalem in whose house Christians gathered to pray, after the arrest of Peter.
Tax collector in Capernaum, called by Jesus to follow him and later counted among the twelve. He is also called Levi. Tradition attributes to him the first gospel.
Disciple chosen by lot to take Judas's place among the twelve apostles.
Offering of flour, oil and incense, made without blood, with salt, in gratitude to God. It could accompany other sacrifices.
Measuring rod of six cubits (about 2.7 m), used in the vision of the temple in Ezekiel.
Kingdom east of Assyria that allied with Babylon in the fall of Nineveh and later united with Persia. The Medes appear in Daniel and in Esther.

Someone who stands between two parties and brings them together. Moses was the mediator of the covenant at Sinai. The New Testament says there is "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus".
Sea west of the land of Israel, called the "Great Sea" in the Bible, which forms the western border of the promised land. Paul crossed it on his journeys.
Disposition of one who does not impose himself by force but trusts in God. It appears among the fruits of the Spirit, and Jesus declares the meek blessed. Moses is called the humblest man on earth.
Fortified city in the valley of Jezreel, site of many battles, among them the death of Josiah. Armageddon, in Revelation, comes from "mountain of Megiddo".
King of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham and received a tithe from him. Hebrews sees in him a figure of the priesthood of Christ.
Ancient capital of Egypt, near present-day Cairo, mentioned by the prophets when announcing judgment on Egypt.
King of Israel who paid tribute of a thousand talents of silver to Pul, king of Assyria.
Son of Jonathan, lame from childhood because of a fall. David welcomed him to his own table in memory of Jonathan and restored to him the lands of Saul.

Compassion in action, especially toward those in need or guilt. It is one of God's main attributes in the Old Testament and is what Jesus asks of his disciples: "Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful."

Gold lid of the ark of the covenant, between two cherubim, where God met with the people and where, on the Day of Atonement, blood was sprinkled. The same Greek word is used for Christ in Romans 3:25.
King of Babylon who sent messengers to Hezekiah after his illness. Isaiah foresaw that the treasures shown to them would be carried to Babylon.
Region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, cradle of great empires (Assyria, Babylon). Abraham came from Ur and from Haran, and Jacob lived in Paddan Aram, in Laban's house.

Hebrew word meaning "anointed", translated into Greek as "Christ". In Israel it designated anointed kings, priests and prophets, and later the promised deliverer. Christians affirm that Jesus is the Messiah.
Son of Enoch, father of Lamech and grandfather of Noah. According to Genesis he lived 969 years, the longest life recorded in the Bible. His name is still used today for a very old person.
Prophet of Judah, a contemporary of Isaiah, who announced that Israel's ruler would come from Bethlehem and summed up what God requires: justice, mercy and humility.
Ephraimite who made a private shrine with idols and hired a Levite as priest. The Danites took the Levite and the idols when they captured Laish.
Prophet who, unlike Ahab's four hundred prophets, announced the king's defeat and death at Ramoth Gilead.
Archangel presented as the "great prince" who protects the people of God, and who in Revelation fights the dragon.
Daughter of Saul and wife of David, who helped him escape from her father.
Region east of the Red Sea, where Moses lived as a shepherd and married Zipporah, daughter of the priest Jethro.
Nomadic desert people, south of Moab. Moses lived among them, and Gideon defeated them.
God of the Ammonites, for whom Solomon also built an altar.
Roman unit of distance of about 1.5 km. Jesus says: "Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two."
Port city of Asia, where Paul said farewell to the elders of Ephesus.
Food of newborns. In the Bible, "milk" is an image of abundance and also of the basic teachings of the faith.

Period of a thousand years mentioned in Revelation 20, in which Christ reigns with his saints. Christians differ on whether it is literal or symbolic, and on whether it precedes or follows the return of Christ.
Unit of weight and value, about half a kilogram of silver. In the parable of Luke 19, the king gives a mina to each servant.
Extraordinary act attributed to God. The Bible also calls them signs, wonders and mighty works. John prefers the term "signs", which point to who Jesus is.
Sister of Moses and Aaron, called a prophetess. She led the women in praise after the crossing of the Red Sea.
Sending with a purpose. In the New Testament, it is the sending of Jesus by the Father and of the disciples by Jesus to announce the gospel to all peoples.
Name of several places. The one in Benjamin was a national gathering point in Samuel's time and later the seat of the governor Gedaliah.
Region east of the Dead Sea, inhabited by descendants of Lot. Ruth was a Moabite.
God of neighboring peoples, to whom children were offered in sacrifice. The law expressly forbids it, and prophets condemned his worship in Judah.
Cousin and guardian of Esther, who guided her and was honored after foiling a conspiracy against the king.
Region where Abraham took Isaac to offer him, and where, according to tradition, Solomon built the temple.

Liberator and lawgiver of Israel. Rescued from the waters, he was raised in Pharaoh's court, called by God at the burning bush, led the people out of Egypt and received the Law at Sinai. He died on Mount Nebo, without entering the promised land.
Inner room of the tabernacle and of the temple, separated by a veil, where the ark of the covenant stood. Only the high priest entered, once a year, on the Day of Atonement.
Mountain on the border of Edom where Aaron died and was succeeded by Eleazar.
Mountain of Moab, from which Moses saw the promised land before he died.
Mountain east of Jerusalem, where Jesus taught about the end times, prayed and from which he ascended to heaven. Gethsemane lies on its slope.
Tiny seed that becomes a large plant. Jesus uses it to speak of the Kingdom that grows from humble beginnings and of faith, even small, that moves mountains.
Aromatic resin used in perfumes, anointing oil and in preparing bodies. It was one of the gifts of the magi and was used in Jesus' burial.
Shrub with aromatic leaves and white flowers. It appears in the prophets' promises of restoration and was used at the Feast of Booths.
In the New Testament, something that was hidden and has been revealed by God, above all the plan of salvation that includes the Gentiles.
Syrian commander healed of leprosy by obeying the prophet Elisha's command to wash seven times in the Jordan. Jesus recalled him as an example that grace reaches foreigners.
Rich sheep breeder in Carmel, rude to David's men and husband of Abigail. He died a few days later, and Abigail became David's wife.
Owner of a vineyard in Jezreel, put to death by order of Jezebel so that King Ahab could take it.
Eldest sons of Aaron and priests. They died when offering "strange fire" before the Lord, an episode that Leviticus presents as a reminder of the holiness of worship.
King of the Ammonites who besieged Jabesh Gilead and wanted to gouge out the eyes of its inhabitants. Saul defeated him, which confirmed him as king.
Prophet whose book announces the fall of Nineveh, capital of Assyria.
City of Galilee where Jesus raised the only son of a widow.
Mother-in-law of Ruth, who returned to Bethlehem after losing her husband and sons in Moab. She asked to be called Mara, "bitter", and later saw her household restored.

Sixth son of Jacob, second of Bilhah, and the tribe that occupied the region around the Sea of Galilee. Matthew sees in Zebulun and Naphtali the fulfillment of the promise of light for "Galilee of the Gentiles".
Prophet in David's court who rebuked him after his sin with Bathsheba, with the parable of the little ewe lamb, and announced the promise of an eternal dynasty.

Israelite of Cana in Galilee, brought to Jesus by Philip, whom Jesus called "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no deceit". Many identify him with the apostle Bartholomew. He was among the disciples after the resurrection.
One from Nazareth, applied to Jesus. In Acts, the followers of Jesus are called the "sect of the Nazarenes". Not to be confused with a Nazirite, who took a special vow.
Small town in Galilee where Jesus grew up. For that reason he was called "Jesus of Nazareth" and his followers were called "Nazarenes".
Person consecrated to God by a vow, who did not drink wine, did not cut the hair and avoided contact with the dead. Samson and Samuel are considered Nazirites.
King of Babylon who destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC and took the Jews into exile. In the book of Daniel he appears as a ruler who learned to acknowledge the power of the Most High God.
Commander of the guard of Nebuchadnezzar who burned the temple and the city of Jerusalem and took the people into exile. He spared Jeremiah.
Pharaoh of Egypt who killed King Josiah at Megiddo, around 609 BC, and later imposed tribute on Judah.
Arid region south of Judah, where Abraham and Isaac lived. The name means "south" or "dry."
Cupbearer of the Persian king who returned to Jerusalem and led the rebuilding of the city walls in fifty-two days.

Image used by Jesus with Nicodemus: one must be "born again" or "from above" to see the Kingdom of God. It points to the work of the Spirit that renews the person. Christians differ on its relation to baptism.
Paul's expression for the new life in Christ and, more broadly, for the final renewal of the world, with "a new heaven and a new earth".
Holy city that, in Revelation, comes down from heaven, where God lives with human beings, without tears, death or mourning. Hebrews speaks of the "heavenly Jerusalem", the city that believers await.

Beginning of each lunar month in Israel, marked with offerings and trumpets. Isaiah criticizes the hypocrisy of those who keep it without justice, and Paul says that the observance of new moons must not be a reason for judgment among Christians.
Second part of the Christian Bible, written in Greek, with 27 books: the four Gospels, Acts, the letters and Revelation.
Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin who visited Jesus by night and heard about the new birth. Later he defended Jesus and helped bury him.
Group condemned in the letters to the churches of Ephesus and Pergamum in Revelation, for practices that the Lord "hates". Nothing is known with certainty about them.
River of Egypt, on whose waters the life of the country depended. Moses was put in a basket among the reeds of the Nile, and the first plague turned its waters to blood.
Descendant of Ham, described in Genesis as "a mighty hunter before the Lord". His kingdom began in Babel and extended to Assyria, where Nineveh and other cities were built.
Capital of Assyria, to which Jonah was sent, and which repented. Later it was the target of the prophet Nahum's announcement of ruin.
First month of the Jewish religious year (March–April), in which Passover is celebrated. Before the exile it was called Abib.
Righteous man of his generation, chosen by God to build the ark and preserve his family and the animals during the flood. After the flood God made a covenant with him, with the rainbow as its sign.
Large wooden boat that Noah built by God's command to save his family and the animals from the flood.
City of priests where David asked the priest Ahimelech for bread. Saul destroyed it in reprisal.
Land east of Eden where Cain went to live after killing Abel.
Number linked to times of testing and preparation: forty days of the flood, forty years in the wilderness, forty days of Jesus in the wilderness.
Number of fullness and perfection in the Bible: seven days of creation, seven letters and seven seals of Revelation. Jesus says that one must forgive "seventy times seven."
Number of fullness and firmness. Jesus was three days in the tomb, and Peter denied him three times. The Trinity, in Christianity, is Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
Number linked to the people of God: twelve tribes of Israel and twelve apostles. In the New Jerusalem there are twelve gates and twelve foundations.

Fourth book of the Bible, which tells of the census of the people and the forty years in the wilderness, between Sinai and the entry into Canaan. It includes the spies, the rebellion of Korah and the story of Balaam.
Father of Joshua, of the tribe of Ephraim.
Song of Simeon on seeing the child Jesus in the temple: "now, Lord, you let your servant depart in peace". It calls Jesus a light for the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.
Solemn declaration that calls on God as witness. The law requires keeping oaths made to the LORD, and Jesus tells the disciples: "Let your 'Yes' be 'Yes,' and your 'No,' 'No.'"
Prophet, author of the shortest book of the Old Testament, which announces judgment on Edom.
Son of Boaz and Ruth and grandfather of David, in the genealogy of Jesus.
Man of Gath in whose house the ark of the covenant stayed three months after the death of Uzzah. The house was blessed.
Heeding God's will in action. Samuel says that obedience is better than sacrifice. Jesus learned obedience and left the example, and asks to be loved by keeping his commandments.

Gift given to God. In the Old Testament, these were the sacrifices and the firstfruits. In the New, Paul speaks of offerings given with joy for the poor, and the widow who gave two small coins is praised by Jesus.
Craftsman of the tribe of Dan, assistant to Bezalel in building the tabernacle.
Oil extracted from the olive, used in food, lighting, anointing and body care. In the parable of the ten virgins, the oil represents preparation.
Perfumed oils used for anointing, at feasts or funerals. Spikenard was an expensive perfume; Mary of Bethany anointed the feet of Jesus with a pound of pure nard.

First part of the Christian Bible, written mostly in Hebrew, with some parts in Aramaic. It has 39 books in the Protestant canon. It tells the creation, the history of Israel, the law, poetry and prophecy.
Mediterranean tree whose fruit provides olive oil. Noah's dove brought an olive branch, a sign that the waters were receding. Paul uses the olive tree as an image of God's people.
Dry measure equal to one tenth of an ephah, about two liters. It was the daily portion of manna for each person.
Commander who became king of Israel and founded Samaria as capital. He was the father of Ahab. Assyrian documents call Israel the "land of Omri".

Number from Revelation that represents the sealed servants of God, twelve thousand from each tribe, and that appears again with the Lamb on Mount Zion. Christians differ on whether the number is literal or symbolic.
Slave of Philemon who ran away, met Paul in prison and was sent back with a letter asking that he be received as a brother.
Christian of Ephesus who was not ashamed of Paul's chains and sought him out in Rome, refreshing him.
Narrow hill south of the temple mount in Jerusalem, part of the city of David, fortified by kings of Judah.
Region famous for fine gold, from which the fleets of Solomon and Hiram came. Its exact location is uncertain.
Moabite daughter-in-law of Naomi, who said farewell to her mother-in-law while Ruth remained with her.
First of the judges of Israel, nephew of Caleb. He conquered Kiriath Sepher, won as his wife Achsah, Caleb's daughter, and delivered the people from the king of Aram Naharaim.
From the Greek "episkopos", "supervisor". In the writings of the New Testament the role merges with that of presbyter or elder, who cared for the local churches.
Tree of warm regions, a symbol of vitality and righteousness. Deborah judged under a palm tree, and the crowd waved palm branches at the entry of Jesus into Jerusalem.
Aquatic plant of the Nile, used to make small boats, baskets and writing material. The basket of Moses was made of papyrus.
Short story, drawn from ordinary life, with which Jesus taught truths about the Kingdom of God. Among the best known are the sower, the good Samaritan and the prodigal son.

Parable of Jesus about a sower whose seed falls on four kinds of soil: beside the path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil. Jesus explains it as the different responses to the word of the Kingdom.

Parable of a master who entrusts talents to three servants before traveling. Two multiply them and are praised; the third buries his and is rebuked. It teaches faithfulness in the use of what we have received.

Word of Persian origin for "garden". In the New Testament, it appears when Jesus promises the repentant thief to be with him "in paradise" and when Paul speaks of being caught up into paradise. It also designates life in God's presence.
Priest and chief of the temple who had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks.

Feast that recalls Israel's deliverance from Egypt, when the angel of death passed over the houses marked with the blood of the lamb. Jesus celebrated the Passover with his disciples at the last supper and is associated with the Lamb of God.
Lamb sacrificed at Passover in memory of the night in Egypt, when the blood on the doors spared the houses of Israel. The New Testament calls Christ "our Passover lamb".
Name given to Paul's letters to Timothy and to Titus, written to church leaders about the care of the flock, sound teaching, the choice of elders and deacons and Christian conduct.
Capacity to wait and endure without giving up. The Bible shows it in Job, in God and in those who wait for the LORD. Patience is among the fruits of the Spirit.
Small island in the Aegean Sea, where the apostle John was exiled when he received the visions of Revelation.

Pharisee of Tarsus, formerly a persecutor of the church, who met Jesus on the road to Damascus and became the great missionary to the Gentiles. He founded communities around the Mediterranean, wrote letters that make up a good part of the New Testament, and was arrested in Jerusalem and taken to Rome. His Hebrew name was Saul.

Paul's travels around the Mediterranean told in Acts: the first journey with Barnabas (Cyprus and Galatia), the second with Silas (Macedonia and Greece), the third (Ephesus and again Greece), and the final voyage to Rome as a prisoner.

Thirteen letters of the New Testament attributed to Paul: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, 1 and 2 Timothy, Titus and Philemon. The letter to the Hebrews was attributed to him in some traditions, but does not carry his name.
In Hebrew, shalom: fullness of life, well-being and good relationship with God and with others. Jesus leaves his peace to the disciples, and Paul speaks of the peace that surpasses all understanding.

Sacrifice of Israel in which part of the animal was burned on the altar and part was eaten by the worshiper in a meal before God, in gratitude and fellowship. It differs from the burnt offering, in which everything was burned.
Jewel taken from the sea, highly valued. Jesus compares the Kingdom to a pearl of great value and warns against throwing pearls before pigs. In Revelation, the gates of the New Jerusalem are pearls.
King of Israel who, with Rezin of Aram, attacked Judah in the time of Ahaz and was killed by Hoshea.
Place on the bank of the Jabbok river, where Jacob wrestled with a divine being and received the name Israel. The name means "face of God".
Second wife of Elkanah, who provoked Hannah because of her barrenness.

One of the two criminals crucified with Jesus, who recognized his innocence and asked: "Remember me". Jesus promised him he would be with him in paradise. The name Dismas comes from later tradition, not from the Bible.
The first five books of the Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy), traditionally attributed to Moses.
Jewish Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, tied to the harvest. In Jerusalem, on that day, the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, and the church appeared publicly.
Region east of the Jordan, south of Galilee, governed by Herod Antipas, where Jesus taught near the end of his ministry.
Twins born to Judah and Tamar. Perez appears in the line of David and of Jesus.
City of Pamphylia through which Paul and Barnabas passed on the first journey; there John Mark left them.
City in Asia, seat of one of the seven churches of Revelation, where "Satan's throne" was. Parchment and a great library came from there.
People of Canaan, named in the lists of the peoples of the promised land. It was present in the land since the time of Abraham.
Hostility suffered because of faith. Jesus warns that his disciples will be persecuted, and the book of Acts shows Stephen, James and Paul being targeted. Peter and Paul teach endurance with hope.
Ability to keep standing firm despite difficulties. Paul says that tribulation produces perseverance, and Revelation promises the crown of life to those faithful until death.
Empire that succeeded Babylon and allowed the Jews to return to Jerusalem. Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes are Persian kings named in the Bible.
Parable of the friend who knocks at midnight asking for bread. It teaches persevering in prayer and trusting that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

Fisherman of Capernaum, brother of Andrew, one of the twelve apostles and spokesman for the disciples. Jesus gave him the name Cephas or Peter, "rock". He denied his Master three times, was restored and led the church in Jerusalem. Two letters of the New Testament bear his name.
Title of the kings of Egypt. In the Bible he appears in the stories of Joseph, of Moses and of the plagues of Egypt.
Parable of two men who pray in the temple: the Pharisee boasts, and the tax collector asks for mercy. The second goes home justified, for "the one who humbles himself will be exalted".

Jewish religious group that valued study and careful observance of the Law and of the traditions of the elders, and believed in the resurrection and in angels. Jesus criticized them for hypocrisy, but some Pharisees followed him, such as Nicodemus and Paul.
City in Asia, seat of one of the seven churches of Revelation, praised for keeping the Lord's word despite having little power.
Christian of Colossae, recipient of Paul's letter on behalf of Onesimus, a runaway slave who had become a useful servant and a brother.
Apostle from Bethsaida, who brought Nathanael to Jesus and whom Jesus questioned before multiplying the loaves. He should not be confused with Philip the evangelist, one of the seven deacons.

One of the seven chosen in Jerusalem for the service to the needy. He preached in Samaria, baptized the Ethiopian eunuch and later lived in Caesarea, where he had four daughters who prophesied. He is distinct from the apostle Philip.
City of Macedonia, the first where Paul preached in Europe. The letter to the Philippians is addressed to the church there.
Coastal region of southwestern Canaan, inhabited by the Philistines, ancient rivals of Israel.
People of the southwest coast of Canaan, enemy of Israel in the time of the judges and of Saul and David. Goliath and Delilah were Philistines.

Grandson of Aaron and priest, remembered for his zeal at Baal Peor, when the plague stopped. He received the promise of a covenant of perpetual priesthood. Another Phinehas was a son of the priest Eli.
Servant (or deaconess) of the church at Cenchrea, commended by Paul and probable bearer of the letter to the Romans.
Seafaring and trading people of the coast of Lebanon, with Tyre and Sidon as principal cities.
Small leather boxes with texts of the law, tied to the arm and the forehead. Jesus criticized those who made their phylacteries broad for show. The tassels on garments recalled the commandments.
Animal considered unclean by Israel's law. In the story of the prodigal son, the young man ends up feeding pigs. Jesus asked not to throw pearls before pigs.
Person who lives as a visitor in a land that is not his own. Abraham and the patriarchs lived as pilgrims. The New Testament calls Christians "pilgrims" who seek a better homeland.
Books of the Old Testament in the form of poetry and wisdom: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Solomon.
Roman governor of Judea who, although declaring Jesus innocent, handed him over to be crucified, yielding to pressure from the chief priests and the crowd.
The needy, whom Israel's law commands to protect and whom the prophets defend. Jesus announces good news to the poor and says that the Kingdom is theirs.
Officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, who bought Joseph as a slave in Egypt. The false accusation made by Potiphar's wife led Joseph to prison.
God's strength and what it accomplishes. The Bible speaks of God's power in creation, in the exodus and in the resurrection. Paul says that the gospel is "the power of God for salvation".
Official residence of the Roman governor. It was there that Jesus was tried and mocked by the soldiers. Paul was also held in custody in Herod's praetorium in Caesarea.
Expression of admiration and gratitude to God in word and song. The book of Psalms is, in Hebrew, "Praises". The word "hallelujah" means "praise the LORD".
Conversation with God, of praise, request, confession and gratitude. The Bible offers the book of Psalms as a school of prayer, and Jesus taught the disciples to pray.

Stones used in adornments and in the breastplate of the high priest, with the names of the twelve tribes. In Revelation, the foundations of the New Jerusalem are made of twelve kinds of precious stones.

Teaching that God determined in advance the destiny of people or of his people. Paul uses the term in Romans and Ephesians. Christian traditions differ on whether it means God's unconditional choice or whether it foresees the human response.
Local leader of New Testament churches. It appears as equivalent to "overseer" (bishop) in some texts. Its task was to teach and to care for the flock.
Excess of self-confidence, which opposes God. Proverbs says that pride goes before destruction, and James affirms that "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble".

Servant of the sanctuary who presented sacrifices and interceded for the people. In Israel, the role belonged to descendants of Aaron. The New Testament calls Christ a high priest and speaks of the "priesthood" of all believers.
Spiritual forces that Paul speaks of. He says that the Christian's struggle is against "principalities and powers" and that Christ triumphed over them on the cross.
Jewish couple, tentmakers and companions of Paul in Corinth and Ephesus, who instructed Apollos and opened their home to the church.
Roman governor of a province. Pontius Pilate was procurator of Judea. Felix and Festus, later procurators, appear in Acts.

Parable of Luke 15 about a son who asks for his inheritance, wastes it in reckless living and returns repentant; the father receives him with a feast, and the older brother resents it. It portrays the Father's love for those who return.
God's commitment to do something. The Bible speaks of promises to Abraham, to David and to the people, and Paul affirms that in Christ "all the promises of God are yes".
Land that God promised to Abraham and his descendants, Canaan, described as a "land flowing with milk and honey". Christians also speak of a heavenly homeland that fulfills this promise.
Inspired message from God, not always about the future: often a call to repentance and justice. In the New Testament, prophecy is also a gift of the Spirit for building up the church.

Person called by God to speak in his name, call the people to faithfulness and announce the future. The "major prophets" are Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel (and Daniel, in some lists), and the twelve "minor prophets" have shorter books.

Gentiles who converted to Judaism, accepting circumcision and the law. There were proselytes in Jerusalem at Pentecost, and Jesus criticized those who made a proselyte "twice as much a son of Gehenna".
Image of Revelation of a woman seated on seven mountains, who represents the corrupt and oppressive city. Ancient Christians identified her with Rome.
Book of maxims of wisdom, attributed in large part to Solomon, which guides practical life with the fear of the Lord.
God's care for his creation and his guidance of events. The story of Joseph shows God turning into good the evil done to him. Jesus says that the Father cares for the birds and the lilies.
Collection of 150 poems, prayers and songs of Israel, in five books. Many are attributed to David. They served as the hymnal of Israel and of the church.
Chief man of the island of Malta who hosted Paul and the shipwrecked. Paul healed his father, who was suffering from fever and dysentery.

Act of making pure. Israel's law prescribed rites of purification for the body and for objects. The New Testament teaches that the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience and calls for purity of heart.
Jewish feast that recalls the book of Esther and the deliverance of the people from Haman's plot.
Expensive dye extracted from mollusks, used in royal fabrics. Lydia sold purple in Philippi, and the soldiers dressed Jesus in a purple robe in mockery.
Roman coin of small value, a quarter of an assarion. Jesus says that no one will get out of prison until he has paid the last quadrans. The widow gave two small coins, which were worth a quadrans.
Ruler who visited Solomon in Jerusalem, drawn by his fame for wisdom, and acknowledged the greatness of God. Jesus mentioned her when speaking of wisdom.

Site near the Dead Sea where, starting in 1947, scrolls of ancient Hebrew texts were found, among them copies of almost all the books of the Old Testament, a thousand years older than the manuscripts known until then.
Title of respect given to teachers, "my master". The disciples and others called Jesus Rabbi, but he told his own not to let themselves be called this out of vanity.
Title of the high Assyrian official who, before Jerusalem, tried to discourage the people and Hezekiah with words of mockery and threat.
Aramaic word of contempt, "empty" or "fool." Jesus says that whoever insults his brother with "raca" is answerable to the council.
Jacob's beloved wife, mother of Joseph and Benjamin. Jacob worked seven years for her and another seven afterward. She died giving birth to Benjamin, near Bethlehem.
Woman of Jericho who hid the Israelite spies and had her family spared when the city fell. She is remembered in the genealogy of Jesus and cited as an example of faith.
Sign of God's covenant with Noah that there would be no other flood. It appears in the visions of Ezekiel and of Revelation around the throne.
City of Samuel, where he was born, lived and was buried. Jeremiah mentions it as the place of weeping of the mothers of Israel, which Matthew ties to the slaughter at Bethlehem.
Store cities that the Hebrews built for Pharaoh in Egypt and from which they departed in the exodus.
Payment that frees a captive or a slave. Israel was "redeemed" from Egypt. Jesus says that he came "to give his life as a ransom for many". "Redemption" is another term.

Word used by many Christians for the event in which believers will be "caught up" to meet the Lord at his coming. Christians differ on when and how this will happen, in relation to the tribulation and the millennium.
Bird that Noah released from the ark and that fed Elijah by the brook Cherith by God's order. Jesus cites it as an example of the Father's care.
Wife of Isaac, mother of Esau and Jacob. She was chosen through a servant of Abraham at a well and, according to the account, came to the marriage with a willing heart.
Restoration of a broken relationship. Paul says that God, in Christ, reconciled the world to himself and gave the church "the ministry of reconciliation".
Heifer without defect, burned outside the camp, whose ashes served to prepare the water of purification for those who had touched a dead body. Hebrews compares it to the blood of Christ.
Sea that Israel crossed on dry ground on leaving Egypt, pursued by Pharaoh's army. The Hebrew expression can be translated literally as "sea of reeds".

Release by payment of a price. In the law, the relative who freed someone from slavery or debt was the "redeemer". The Bible uses the image for the deliverance from Egypt and, in the New Testament, for the work of Christ.
Complete renewal by the work of God. Paul speaks of "the washing of regeneration" and Jesus speaks of a "regeneration" when he sits on the throne of his glory.
Son and successor of Solomon. By refusing the request to ease the taxes, he saw ten tribes split off under Jeroboam and was left with only Judah and Benjamin.
Part of God's people who remain faithful or survive a judgment and become the basis of restoration.
Change of mind and of direction, with sorrow for sin and a return to God. In Greek, "metanoia". It was the first message of John the Baptist and of Jesus.
Ancient people of great stature, named in Genesis and in Deuteronomy. Og, king of Bashan, was a descendant of the last of the Rephaim.
Place in the wilderness where Israel complained about the lack of water, Moses brought water out of the rock and Israel fought the Amalekites.
Return to the original state or to fullness. The prophets announce the restoration of Israel after the exile. Peter speaks of "the times of restoring all things".
Return from death to life, in a new body. The gospels affirm that Jesus rose on the third day. Paul sees in the resurrection of Christ the guarantee of the resurrection of believers.
God's just response to what each one has done. The Bible speaks of reward for good and punishment for evil, and Paul says that God "will pay back to everyone according to their works".
Eldest son of Jacob and Leah, who pleaded for Joseph and lost the birthright.
Act by which God makes himself known. Hebrews says that God spoke long ago by the prophets and, in these last days, by the Son. The last book of the Bible is called "Revelation" or "Apocalypse".
The Bible sees wealth as a gift from God and as a danger. Proverbs, the prophets and Jesus warn against trusting in possessions. Jesus said that it is hard for a rich person to enter the Kingdom.
Parable of the rich man who builds bigger barns to store his harvest and dies that night. Jesus teaches that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.

Parable of the rich man who ignores the beggar Lazarus at his door and, after death, suffers in Hades, while Lazarus is comforted. It teaches responsibility toward the needy and the sufficiency of the Law and the Prophets.
Person who lives uprightly before God. Noah, Job and Joseph are called righteous. Paul teaches that no one is righteous by himself and that righteousness comes through faith in Christ.

In the Bible, tied to God's faithfulness to his covenant and to the upright conduct he expects of the people, especially toward the poor, orphans and widows. It is also the condition of one who is in right relationship with God.
Image of security and refuge: the LORD is "my rock". Paul says that the rock that accompanied Israel in the wilderness was Christ, and Jesus says that he will build his church on "this rock".
People of the Roman Empire, which ruled Palestine in the time of Jesus, with governors and soldiers. Paul was a Roman citizen, which gave him rights in his trials.
Capital of the Roman Empire, where Paul was taken as a prisoner. The letter to the Romans was addressed to the church that was there.
Bird whose crow marked the dawn. Jesus foretold that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed.
Flower of the plain of Sharon, mentioned in the Song of Solomon as an image of the beauty of the beloved. Some identify it with a kind of crocus or narcissus.
Christian greeted in Romans, whose mother Paul calls also "mother to me". He may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, mentioned by Mark.

Moabite woman who stayed with her mother-in-law Naomi after her husband's death, saying "your people will be my people". She married Boaz and was the great-grandmother of David. Her book tells a story of loyalty and redemption.

Seventh day of the week, a day of rest made holy by God, recalled in creation and in the fourth commandment. Jesus taught that "the Sabbath was made for man". The early Christians also began to meet on the first day of the week.
Distance that was permitted to walk on the Sabbath, about 900 m. The Mount of Olives was a Sabbath day's journey from Jerusalem.
Every seven years, the land was to rest and debts were forgiven. It was a reminder that the land belongs to God and a protection for the poor.
Sign of mourning and repentance: wearing coarse clothing and sitting on ashes or throwing them on the head.

Offering presented to God in worship, in thanksgiving or as reparation for sin, in the temple and the tabernacle. The New Testament speaks of the sacrifice of Christ and of the "living sacrifice" that believers offer.
Group of the priestly elite in Jerusalem, tied to the temple. They accepted only the written Law and denied the resurrection and angels.

In the New Testament, "saints" are Christians in general, set apart for God, and not only exceptional people. Paul writes "to the saints" of each church. Later traditions use the word in different ways.
Woman who followed Jesus, identified with the mother of James and John. She was at the cross and went with other women to the tomb on Sunday.
Salome mother of the sons of Zebedee
Used for seasoning and preserving. In the law, offerings had to include salt. Jesus calls the disciples the "salt of the earth", and Paul recommends words "seasoned with salt".
Deliverance granted by God, in several senses: from danger, from oppression, from sin and from death. In the New Testament it is linked to the person and work of Jesus, called Savior.
Central region between Galilee and Judea, inhabited by Samaritans, who had difficult relations with the Jews. Also the name of the capital of the northern kingdom.
Inhabitant of the region of Samaria, of mixed origin, who worshiped on Mount Gerizim. Jesus told the parable of the good Samaritan and talked with the Samaritan woman.
Woman whom Jesus met at Jacob's well, in Sychar. He spoke to her of "living water" and of worship "in spirit and truth", and she led many Samaritans to him.

People of Samaria who accepted only the Pentateuch and worshiped on Mount Gerizim. The Jews avoided them. Jesus treated them with respect: he healed a Samaritan leper, talked with the Samaritan woman and made a Samaritan the model of a neighbor.
Judge of Israel, a Nazirite from birth, known for his great strength, which was tied to his hair. He was betrayed by Delilah and died pulling down the temple of the Philistines.
Last of the judges, prophet and priest, dedicated to God by his mother Hannah. He anointed the first two kings of Israel, Saul and David.
Governor of Samaria who, with Tobiah and Geshem, mocked and opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls in the time of Nehemiah.
Process or state of one who has been set apart for God. In Hebrew, "holy" means set apart, dedicated. God is holy and calls his people to holiness in all they do.
Simple footwear. Taking them off was a sign of reverence, as with Moses before the bush. John the Baptist said he was not worthy to untie the straps of the sandals of Jesus.
Supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, made up of priests, elders and scribes, presided over by the high priest. It tried Jesus, Stephen and Paul.
Wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac, who was born when she was already old, as God had promised. Her original name was Sarai. She was buried in the cave of Machpelah, in Hebron.
City in Asia, seat of one of the seven churches, rebuked for having a name of being alive while being dead.
Adversary of God and accuser of human beings. He appears in Job, in the temptation of Jesus and in Revelation. "Satan" comes from the Hebrew for "adversary", and "devil" from the Greek for "accuser".
First king of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, anointed by Samuel. He was rejected by God after disobeying and persecuted David. He died in battle against the Philistines at Gilboa.
On the Day of Atonement, two goats were used: one was sacrificed, and over the other the high priest confessed the sins of the people and sent it into the wilderness, symbolically carrying them away.
Staff of authority of a king. The promise given to Judah speaks of the scepter that would not depart from him. The scepter of righteousness belongs to the Messiah.
Venomous arachnid of the desert, an image of pain and punishment. Jesus gave the disciples authority to tread on "serpents and scorpions".
Scholars and copyists of the Law, who interpreted and taught it. The gospels mention them alongside the Pharisees and the chief priests.
Large freshwater lake in northern Israel, also called the Sea of Tiberias or Gennesaret. On its shores Jesus called fishermen, taught and calmed a storm.
Measure of capacity equal to one third of an ephah, about seven liters. Sarah used three seahs of fine flour for the visitors.

Sign of authenticity and ownership. Paul says that Christians were "sealed with the Holy Spirit" as a guarantee of the inheritance. In Revelation, seals close the book and God's servants receive a seal on their foreheads.
Second and Third Letters of John
Two short letters of the apostle John: the second, to a "chosen lady" and her children, warns against false teachers; the third, to his friend Gaius, praises hospitality and criticizes Diotrephes.
Return of Christ at the end of time, awaited by the church. The Greek word "parousia" means "presence" or "arrival".
Farewell letter of Peter, which warns against false teachers and reminds that the Lord is not slow in keeping his promises.
Letter from Paul in which he defends his ministry, speaks of comfort in suffering, of the collection for Jerusalem and of the strength that is made perfect in weakness.
Letter that corrects misunderstandings about the day of the Lord and urges those who were not working to earn their own bread.
Letter traditionally held to be the last of Paul, written from prison, in which he encourages Timothy to remain firm and to pass on the teaching.

Word used for descendants. The promise made to Abraham and to his "seed" is interpreted by Paul as fulfilled in Christ. Jesus uses the image of the seed in the parable of the sower and to speak of his own death.
Mountainous region south of the Dead Sea, where Esau and the Edomites settled.
Hebrew term that appears in the Psalms and in Habakkuk, generally understood as a pause or emphasis in the music or reading, to meditate. Its exact meaning is uncertain.
King of Assyria who invaded Judah in the time of Hezekiah, took fortified cities and surrounded Jerusalem. He returned to Nineveh after a great loss in the army and was assassinated by his own sons.
Greek translation of the Old Testament, made in Alexandria from the third century BC. It was the Bible used by many authors of the New Testament and by the first Christian communities.
Six-winged heavenly beings who, in the vision of the temple, sang "Holy, holy, holy" and purified Isaiah's lips with a coal.
Roman proconsul of Cyprus, an intelligent man, who believed after Paul struck the sorcerer Elymas blind for a time.
Great discourse of Jesus in Matthew 5 to 7, with the beatitudes, the teaching on the law, prayer and trust in God.
Animal that appears in Genesis 3 as the tempter. Moses lifted up a bronze serpent, and Jesus says that the disciples must be "wise as serpents and harmless as doves".
Title given to those who serve God: Moses, David, the prophets. Paul and James present themselves as servants of Christ. Jesus himself said that he came "not to be served, but to serve".
Son of Adam and Eve, born after Abel's death. The line that leads to Noah descends from him, and in his time people "began to call on the name of the Lord".
The seven churches of the province of Asia to which the letters of Revelation 2 and 3 are addressed: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea.
In Revelation, three series of seven judgments: the seals opened by the Lamb, the trumpets and the bowls. They show God's action in history and at its end.
Group of disciples whom Jesus sent, two by two, ahead of him, to announce the Kingdom. The number varies between 70 and 72 in the ancient manuscripts.
Image of God's protection ("under the shadow of your wings") and also of something that foreshadows the reality, as in the law, a "shadow of the good things to come".
Three young Jews at the court of Babylon, companions of Daniel, who refused to worship the golden statue and were thrown into the furnace, from which they came out unharmed.
King of Assyria who besieged Samaria. The final fall of the city, around 722 BC, ended the northern kingdom, and the population was taken captive.
Hebrew word of greeting, translated "peace". It designates complete well-being, health, harmony and a restored relationship with God and with others.
Scribe of King Josiah, who read to the king the book of the law found in the temple. His family supported the prophet Jeremiah.
Fertile coastal plain between Joppa and Mount Carmel, famous for its flowers and pastures.
Kingdom of southern Arabia, famous for the trade in gold and spices. From it came the queen who visited Solomon.
Central city of Israel, where Abraham built an altar, Jacob bought land and Joseph was buried. Joshua renewed the covenant there.

Flock animal, dependent on the shepherd. The psalms and the prophets call God's people "sheep", and Jesus presents himself as the good shepherd. Isaiah compares the suffering servant to the sheep led to the slaughter.

Description of the final judgment in which the Son of Man separates the sheep from the goats according to the care they showed for the hungry, thirsty, foreigners, naked, sick and imprisoned: "Whatever you did to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me".
Measure of weight and silver coin, about 11 grams. It was used to pay for purchases and for the temple tax.
Eldest son of Noah, ancestor of the peoples called Semites, including the Hebrews. The word "Semitic" comes from his name. Abraham descends from his line.
Dwelling of the dead in the Old Testament, described as a place of silence. In the Greek translation it appears as "Hades", used in the New Testament.
Region of low hills between the mountains of Judah and the coastal plain, a zone of conflicts with the Philistines.
One who cares for sheep. In the Bible the term is used for God, for kings and leaders and for Jesus himself, "the good shepherd".
Prince of Judah to whom Cyrus handed the temple vessels and who led the first group of exiles back to Jerusalem.
City where the tabernacle stood for a long time, before the temple was built in Jerusalem. There Samuel served Eli.
Benjamite of Saul's family who cursed David on his flight from Jerusalem. David spared him, but Solomon had him executed after he disobeyed the order not to leave the city.
Region of Mesopotamia where Babel stood; it corresponds to the plain of Babylon.
Pharaoh of Egypt who invaded Judah in the fifth year of Rehoboam and took treasures from the temple.
Place on the plain of Moab, where Israel camped before crossing the Jordan and from which Joshua sent the spies to Jericho.
Trumpet made of a ram's horn, used to give signals, to summon the people and to announce feasts. The walls of Jericho fell at its sound. It is blown at the Jewish New Year.
Table of acacia wood overlaid with gold, in the holy place, on which twelve loaves were placed, a symbol of the twelve tribes. See also "Bread of the Presence".
Woman of Shunem who hosted the prophet Elisha and received the promise of a son. When the boy died, Elisha raised him.
Greek word for "assassins," from the Latin sica, the dagger. It also designates a Jewish revolutionary group. The Roman tribune believed that Paul was an Egyptian who had led four thousand sicarii.
Phoenician city, beside Tyre, rich in trade and navigation. Jesus cites it as an example of a city that would have repented if it had seen his miracles.
Extraordinary act that reveals the power of God. John calls the miracles of Jesus "signs", which point to who he is.
Ring used as a seal on documents, a symbol of authority. Pharaoh gave Joseph his ring, and King Ahasuerus handed his to Haman and later to Mordecai.
Amorite kings east of the Jordan, defeated by Israel before the crossing: Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, the last of the Rephaim. The victory is remembered in the Psalms.
Prophet of the church in Jerusalem, companion of Paul on the second missionary journey. He was imprisoned with him in Philippi.
Pool of Jerusalem, connected by a tunnel to the spring of Gihon, built in the time of Hezekiah. Jesus told the man born blind to wash there.
Precious metal, used as money and in objects of worship. Judas betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver. Proverbs compares wisdom to silver.
Righteous and devout man of Jerusalem who took the child Jesus in his arms in the temple and praised God. His song is the Nunc Dimittis.
Second son of Jacob and Leah. With Levi he avenged his sister Dinah in Shechem, and for that Jacob rebuked him on his deathbed. His tribe received land within the territory of Judah, in the south.
Man who was forced by the soldiers to carry Jesus' cross.
Man of Bethany in whose house a woman anointed Jesus with costly perfume, a few days before the Passover.
Pharisee who invited Jesus to dinner and was scandalized when a sinful woman anointed his feet. Jesus responded with the parable of the two debtors.

Man of Samaria who practiced magic and, seeing the Spirit given by the laying on of the apostles' hands, wanted to buy that power. Peter rebuked him. From him comes the term "simony", trade in sacred things.
One of the twelve apostles, called "the Zealot", a term that recalls the nationalist movement that fought against Rome, or zeal for the Law.

Failure toward God: disobedience, injustice or turning away from his will. In Hebrew and Greek the word recalls "missing the mark". The New Testament teaches that all have sinned and that Christ brought forgiveness.
Sacrifice prescribed to deal with sins committed unintentionally and with impurities, restoring the relationship with God. The guilt offering also included making amends for the damage done.
Mountain in the desert where God revealed himself to Moses and gave the Law to the people, after the exodus. Also called Horeb.
Distant land mentioned by Isaiah as a place from which the exiles would come, usually associated with southern Egypt or a land of the east.
Commander of the army of Jabin, king of Canaan, with nine hundred iron chariots. He was defeated by Deborah and Barak and killed by Jael.

Condition of someone who belongs to another. Israel's law regulated slavery and protected the slave. The New Testament uses the image to speak of liberation from sin and of service to Christ. Paul calls himself a "slave of Christ".
City in Asia, seat of one of the seven churches of Revelation. It was praised for its faithfulness in the midst of persecution.
Cities of the Jordan plain destroyed by fire and sulfur because of the wickedness of their inhabitants. Abraham interceded for them.

Son of David and Bathsheba, third king of Israel. He asked God for wisdom, built the temple in Jerusalem and is remembered for Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes. His reign ended with the division of the kingdom after his death.
Colonnade on the east side of the temple of Jerusalem, where Jesus walked and where the first Christians gathered.
Title of Jesus as the Messiah descended from David, to whom an eternal kingdom was promised. The blind and the crowds call him this, and Matthew opens his Gospel with this expression.

Title of Jesus in the Gospels, which expresses his unique relationship with the Father. In the Old Testament, the title was also applied to Israel, to the Davidic king and to the angels. The Father declares him "my beloved Son" at the baptism and at the transfiguration.
Title that Jesus used for himself, originating in Daniel's vision of one "like a son of man" who receives everlasting dominion. It points both to humanity and to authority.
Book of love poetry attributed to Solomon, read both as a celebration of human love and as an image of the love between God and his people.
Belief that God rules over everything. The psalms proclaim him king over all the nations, and Daniel acknowledges that "the Most High rules in the kingdom of men".
Measure of length, the width of the open hand, about 22 centimeters (9 inches), equivalent to half a cubit.
Small and common bird. Jesus says that no sparrow falls without the Father knowing and that the disciples are worth more than many sparrows.

The twelve men sent by Moses, one from each tribe, to examine Canaan. Ten brought back a report of fear; only Joshua and Caleb trusted the promise, and the unbelieving generation had to wander forty years in the wilderness. Joshua also sent two spies to Jericho, welcomed by Rahab.
Word that can mean the breath of life, the inner part of a person, spiritual beings or the Spirit of God. The Hebrew ruach and the Greek pneuma also mean "wind" and "breath".

Abilities given by the Holy Spirit to the church for mutual service, such as teaching, serving, prophecy, healings and administration. Paul says there are varieties of gifts but one Spirit, and that love is the most excellent way.
Greek measure of distance, about 185 meters (600 feet). In Luke and in John it is used for distances around Jerusalem and on the Sea of Galilee.
Shepherd's stick for guiding and defending the sheep. It is an image of God's care in Psalm 23. The staff of Moses and Aaron appears in the plagues.
Greek silver coin worth four drachmas. Jesus told Peter to catch a fish in whose mouth he would find a stater to pay the temple tax for the two of them.
First convert in Achaia, whose household "devoted themselves to the service of the saints". He visited Paul in Ephesus.
One of the seven chosen for the service of the tables in Jerusalem. He was stoned after a speech before the Sanhedrin and is considered the first Christian martyr.
Name of places: one in Egypt, first stop of the exodus, and another east of the Jordan, where Jacob made booths.
Experience of pain and loss, to which the Bible gives much space, in Job, in the Psalms and in Lamentations. The New Testament links suffering to that of Christ and to the hope of glory.
Figure of the "Servant songs" of Isaiah, especially Isaiah 52:13-53:12, who suffers for the people. The New Testament applies these texts to Jesus.
Episode in which Joshua prayed at Gibeon and the sun and the moon stood still until Israel defeated the Amorites. One of the most debated accounts of the Old Testament.
One of the women who accompanied Jesus and supported him with their means, mentioned only by Luke.
Wild fig tree of large size and small fruits. Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore to see Jesus, and Amos was a dresser of sycamore figs.
City of Samaria, near Jacob's well, where Jesus spoke with the Samaritan woman.
Jewish meeting house for reading the Scriptures, prayer and teaching, probably arising during the exile. Jesus and Paul attended synagogues.
The first three gospels (Matthew, Mark and Luke), which tell the life of Jesus in a similar way, "with the same view".
Canaanite city in the valley of Jezreel, near which Deborah and Barak fought.
Portable sanctuary that Israel carried through the wilderness, made according to the pattern shown to Moses. It had the courtyard, the holy place and the most holy place, where the ark stood.
Disciple in Joppa, known for her good works and charity, raised by Peter.
Mountain in Galilee, associated since antiquity with the episode of Deborah and with the transfiguration of Jesus.
Largest unit of weight and money, about 34 kilograms (75 pounds). In Matthew, the parable of the talents speaks of a great sum entrusted to servants.
Aramaic phrases of Jesus when raising the daughter of Jairus, translated: "Little girl, I tell you, get up!"

Daughter-in-law of Judah, widow of two of his sons, who confronted him on realizing that he was not fulfilling the duty of levirate marriage. From her union with Judah were born Perez and Zerah, in the line of David and of Jesus. A daughter of David, violated by her half-brother Amnon, is also called Tamar.
Percussion instrument played at feasts and dances. Miriam and the women of Israel danced with tambourines after the crossing of the Red Sea.
Babylonian god of vegetation, for whom the women wept. Ezekiel saw in a vision women weeping for Tammuz at the gate of the temple.
Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible, formed from the initials of Torah (Law), Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). Jesus refers to this division in Luke 24:44.
Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Scriptures, read in the synagogues for the people who no longer understood Hebrew well.
Distant city or region, in the far west, to which Jonah tried to flee. It was associated with ships and metals.
City of Cilicia, Paul's native city, famous for its culture and schools.

Amount charged by the authorities. The Jews paid the temple tax and tribute to Rome, which provoked resentment. Jesus taught: "Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's".
Tax collector in the service of Rome, despised by the Jews for cooperating with the foreign power and for demanding more than was due. Jesus called tax collectors such as Matthew and Zacchaeus.
Specialist in the law of Moses, who taught and interpreted the law. He appears in the Gospels alongside scribes and Pharisees. Gamaliel was a respected teacher of the law.
Oasis of northern Arabia, on the caravan route, mentioned in Job and in the prophets. Dedan was another trading center of the same region.

House of worship built in Jerusalem by Solomon, destroyed by the Babylonians, rebuilt after the exile and renovated by Herod. It was destroyed by the Romans in AD 70. The New Testament also speaks of the community and of the believer's body as a temple of the Spirit.
Trial that can lead to sin. Jesus was tempted in the wilderness. James says that God tempts no one, and Paul promises that God will provide a way out for those who are tempted.
Forty days of fasting in the wilderness after the baptism, during which the devil tempted him three times. Jesus answered by quoting Deuteronomy.
Ten punishments that God sent on Egypt through Moses to free Israel: water into blood, frogs, lice, flies, plague on the livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness and the death of the firstborn.
Parable of ten young women waiting for the bridegroom, five wise, who had oil, and five foolish, who did not. It teaches watchfulness and preparation for the return of the Lord.
Father of Abraham, who left Ur and arrived at Haran with his family.
Scribe who wrote the letter to the Romans as Paul dictated it and added his own greeting.
Lawyer who accused Paul before the governor Felix.
Word that translates "covenant". Old and New Testament mean old and new covenant. In Hebrews, it also has the sense of a will that takes effect at the death of the one who made it.
Ruler of a fourth part of a territory. Herod Antipas was tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, and Philip governed the region to the northeast.
